title: Resurgence of Russian attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure affect essential needs, socioeconomic conditions, and humanitarian operations after the end of the partial ceasefire in late April 2025
risk_type: Future impact of a hazard which has already taken place
rationale:
On 25 March 2025, the new US administration – under President Donald Trump – reached an agreement with Ukraine and Russia on a temporary 30-day pause in attacks on energy infrastructure. Ukraine agreed with the US on a list of energy facilities that Russia should stop attacking, although Russia took some oil and gas production facilities off the list and has continued attacking them.
It is unclear whether this partial ceasefire applies to the use of long-range missiles and drones or artillery. The full details of the partial ceasefire have not been made public. Energy infrastructure located near the front line remains vulnerable to damage.
Given the history of Russian forces violating ceasefire agreements since 2014, they are likely to also violate this agreement and resort to disinformation and false flag attacks to conceal the violations, possibly blaming Ukraine for disrupting the ceasefire agreement. In this context, US officials may downplay these violations to claim the success of the US-led ceasefire.
Russian forces, having stockpiled missiles and drones for use against the energy sector, may step up their attacks on civilian infrastructure, such as residential areas, as a sustained political tactic especially following the US-led negotiations for a full ceasefire. A recent such attack was on 4 April, which targeted a residential area in Kryvyi Rih city, Dnipropetrovska, killing 19 people (including 9 children). Alternatively, Russian forces could accumulate the missiles and drones that they planned to use in 2024 then launch a major countrywide combined missile and drone attack against Ukraine’s energy infrastructure immediately after the partial ceasefire ends in late April while also stalling negotiations. ([ACAPS 13/09/2024](https://www.acaps.org/fileadmin/Data_Product/Main_media/20240913_ACAPS_Ukraine_Analysis_hub_Attacks_on_the_energy_infrastructure_in_Ukraine.pdf), [ACAPS 12/02/2025](https://www.acaps.org/fileadmin/Data_Product/Main_media/20250219_ACAPS_Ukraine_-_Energy_infrastructure_attacks-_Updated_outlook_and_impact_during_the_2024-2025_cold_season_.pdf), [Dixigroup 31/03/2025](https://dixigroup.org/en/analytic/russian-war-against-ukraine-energy-dimension-dixi-group-alert-weekly-review-93/), [Kyiv Independent 03/04/2025](https://kyivindependent.com/ukraine-informs-us-about-russias-energy-ceasefire-violations/))
hazard_materialisation:
The risk of large-scale civilian harm in Ukraine is steadily materialising as Russian forces intensify attacks on densely populated areas and critical infrastructure alongside US-led peace negotiations. Civilians have born the brunt of these hostilities, with repeated missile and drone strikes since April 2025 causing mass casualties, widespread destruction, and compounding humanitarian vulnerabilities.
Throughout April 2025, ballistic and aerial strikes frequently targeted residential areas, leading to exceptionally high civilian casualties, including a significant number of children, and marking one of the deadliest months since the escalation of the conflict. Notably, a wave of coordinated attacks on 24 April struck multiple oblasts across the country, inflicting dozens of deaths and hundreds of injuries while devastating residential structures and essential infrastructure. This surge coincided with heightened ceasefire diplomacy, suggesting that military escalation may have accompanied negotiations. Data collected during this period points to an overall rise in damage to civilian infrastructure compared with previous months.
A second escalation phase unfolded in May, characterised by consecutive nationwide strikes coinciding with a major prisoner exchange, the largest since 2014. Despite agreements for regular exchanges having been brokered in advance, the timing reinforces the pattern of intensified attacks during politically significant moments, including foreign-mediated talks. This trend persisted into June, when Russia markedly shifted focus to energy networks and agricultural sites. Critical infrastructure in Khersonska and Poltavska oblasts was severely damaged, while high-precision missile strikes on Kyiv and Odeska oblasts repeatedly struck residential buildings and even medical facilities. A missile strike on Dnipro on 24 June alone caused over 300 civilian casualties, underlining the increasingly indiscriminate and destructive nature of the campaign. By the end of that month, the sustained targeting of energy facilities led to rolling blackouts that deepened civilian hardship.
The scale of attacks further intensified during July. Mass strikes employing hundreds of drones and missiles repeatedly targeted Kyiv and other urban centres, with devastating consequences for civilians. Attacks directly striking residential buildings in Kharkivska and Kyiv oblasts resulted in dozens to more than a hundred casualties in a single incident. These escalations repeatedly coincided with milestones in US-led negotiations, including the Istanbul talks and public statements from US officials warning of sanction deadlines, reinforcing the link between diplomatic events and heightened violence.
In late August, the attacks reached unprecedented levels, with Russian forces deploying hundreds of drones and dozens of missiles in a single day. High-precision strikes on Kyiv oblast killed and injured many civilians, while attacks on energy and gas infrastructure in multiple oblasts left over 100,000 people without power. The systematic targeting of both residential and critical infrastructure confirmed the sustained strategy of leveraging military pressure to influence negotiation dynamics while maximising civilian suffering.
Taken together, this sustained campaign has transformed from a succession of isolated strikes into a persistent pattern of large-scale hostilities against civilians and essential services. The increasing frequency, geographic spread, and strategic timing of the attacks, particularly around peace negotiations and prisoner exchanges, demonstrate a deliberate escalation strategy. This materialisation of risk is evidenced by rising casualty figures, compounded infrastructure damage, and growing humanitarian consequences for millions of civilians caught between military offensives and the fragile negotiation process. ([France 24 27/08/2025](https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20250827-more-than-100-000-ukrainian-homes-lose-power-as-russia-targets-energy-sites), [TKI 28/08/2025](https://kyivindependent.com/russia-drones-target-kyiv-ukrainian-cities-in-large-scale-attack/), [TKI 31/01/2025](https://kyivindependent.com/massive-fires-reported-in-kyiv-amid-russias-latest-drone-attack/), [TKI 23/07/2025](https://kyivindependent.com/breaking-third-round-of-ukraine-russia-negotiations-begin-in-istanbul/))

title: The consolidation of power by Dbeibeh's forces across Libya provokes counteractions from other factions, renewing clashes and protection risks
rationale:
On 12 May 2025, Tripoli security forces announced the killing of Abdel Ghani al-Kikli (also known as Ghnewa), commander of the Stability Support Apparatus (SSA). His assassination immediately triggered armed clashes in southern Tripoli. Militia units loyal to the SSA fought the 444th Combat Brigade forces (aligned with Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah), resulting in intense gun battles and killing eight civilians. By 14 May, a ceasefire was declared. As part of the political impacts, Tripoli saw large protests with demonstrators demanding Dbeibah’s resignation. By mid-May, at least three ministers announced their resignations in solidarity with the protesters.
In eastern Libya, the Libyan National Army (LNA) remains under the control of General Khalifa Haftar, with his son, Lieutenant General Saddam Haftar, taking on an increasingly central operational role. In April 2025, Saddam held meetings in Ankara and Washington, signalling growing diplomatic outreach. Domestically, he has overseen new military deployments and Russian arms deliveries since December 2024. On 20 May 2025, LNA patrols under his command were reported deploying towards southwest Libya, likely indicating a strategic shift of eastern forces to the southern region. With Dbeibah's recent consolidation of power in Tripoli and Ghnewa’s defeat, Saddam may likely be preparing for a countermove. Drawing on past events, such as in 2019 when Khalifa Haftar led a military campaign to control Tripoli but failed, Saddam could escalate militarily through deployments from Sebha or Sirte districts or by mobilising southern tribal militias. His actions indicate readiness to exploit any perceived weakness in the Tripoli-based Government of National Unity.
Any prolonged fighting in Tripoli is likely to draw in external factions and lead to militia skirmishes extending beyond Tripoli into Zawiya and Misrata cities or some cities in Fezzan region, or provoke direct LNA intervention from the east or south. For instance, units from Zawiya and Warshefana were seen moving towards Tripoli during the recent clashes in May. The clashes could shift from being between militias to involving more formal forces, such as the LNA’s southern brigades, resulting in fighting erupting in civilian neighbourhoods and leading to displacement. ([Atlantic Council 16/05/2025](https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/blogs/menasource/the-killing-of-abdul-ghani-al-kikli-may-be-a-turning-point-for-libya/#:~:text=On%20May%2012%2C%202025%2C%20Abdulghani,%E2%80%9Dhttps://www.hrw.org/news/2025/05/20/libya-civilians-caught-militia-clashes#:~:text=Heavy%20fighting%20broke%20out%20between,government), [Reuters 16/05/2025](https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/middle-east/two-ministers-internationally-recognized-libyan-government-resign-2025-05-16/), [AJ 17/05/2025](https://aje.io/3tcjm6))

title: Contested electoral process ahead of Côte d'Ivoire’s October 2025 elections leads to political violence and protection risks
rationale:
Côte d’Ivoire is preparing for presidential elections scheduled for 25 October 2025. Although recent elections have been relatively peaceful, the political environment is becoming increasingly tense. The Independent Electoral Commission (CEI) released the final electoral roll on 4 June, confirming the exclusion of four prominent opposition leaders: Laurent Gbagbo, Tidjane Thiam, Charles Blé Goudé, and Guillaume Soro. While Thiam was excluded based on nationality concerns, the others were barred because of past judicial convictions. All four are also prohibited from voting.
The exclusion of these high-profile figures has triggered strong criticism from their parties, which have withdrawn from the CEI and denounced a lack of institutional independence. Some, such as Thiam and his party, have appealed to international bodies such as the UNHRC. Others, including former first lady Simone Gbagbo, have warned that the conditions are not in place for peaceful elections. Some parties have announced protests, and public calls for boycotts or civil disobedience could escalate in the coming months.
The memory of the 2010–2011 post-electoral crisis, which caused over 3,000 civilian deaths, still shapes public perception. While today’s situation differs—institutions are more stable, and international scrutiny is higher—the exclusionary political landscape and growing polarisation echo the warning signs of past unrest. The delayed announcement of President Ouattara’s candidacy adds further uncertainty. If he decides to run for a fourth term, in potential breach of constitutional limits, it could become a flashpoint. title: Intensifying humanitarian and security crisis in Kenya worsens conditions in refugee camps
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale:
Kenya’s refugee camps, particularly Dadaab and Kakuma, are facing an increasingly fragile situation owing to severe underfunding, overstretched infrastructure, and surging new arrivals. Cuts in humanitarian aid have already led to reductions in food rations, the closure of essential services, and growing frustration among both refugees and host communities. In 2025, WFP was only able to provide 60% of the minimum food basket by midyear, with responders reporting critical gaps in healthcare, education, and WASH services. The camps, which host more than 600,000 refugees, are still absorbing new displacements from conflict-affected areas of Ethiopia, Somalia, and Sudan. These arrivals further strain already limited resources and contribute to tensions over land, water, and security. Escalating tensions have already led to ethnic clashes, protests, and police interventions within camps including Kakuma and Dadaab. Without urgent interventions, the situation risks spiralling into a protracted crisis marked by localised violence, cross-border insecurity, or forced returns, particularly in light of Kenya's shifting asylum policies and security stance in border regions.
Gaps in healthcare access are increasing the risk of disease outbreaks, particularly as overcrowded living conditions and limited water supplies worsen. Economic hardship and congested settlements are also heightening protection concerns, including gender-based violence. As services and water availability decline, households are expected to relocate within or between camps in search of support, further straining space and social cohesion.
Kenya’s Shirika Plan also continues to face implementation hurdles and growing scepticism among host communities related to resource competition and security. There are concerns that the plan will only benefit those already with resources (business owners and skilled people) rather than the most vulnerable. Given that, the situation may evolve into a sustained protection and humanitarian crisis marked by deteriorating health conditions, rising insecurity, and the potential for forced or premature returns. Refugees may increasingly move outside formal camps in search of livelihoods or better services, often without documentation or assistance. This trend could heighten risks of exploitation, detention, or deportation and further complicate humanitarian coordination and protection efforts. ([TNH 23/05/2025](https://www.thenewhumanitarian.org/news-feature/2025/05/23/dadaab-voices-what-aid-cuts-mean-kenyas-refugees), [AJ 20/07/2025](https://liberties.aljazeera.com/en/refugees-in-kenya-face-deepening-hunger-as-aid-cuts-bite/)
hazard_materialisation: Kenya’s humanitarian and security situation deteriorates, particularly in refugee-hosting areas such as Garissa and Turkana counties. This systemic breakdown in assistance created a volatile environment, heightening tensions between refugees and host communities, and sparking protests and violent clashes, such as those in Kalobeyei in late June 2025. At the same time, rising insecurity, resource scarcity, and disease outbreaks including dengue fever in Dadaab have compounded the fragility of the camps.
impact_materialisation_description: The situation in Kenya’s refugee-hosting areas has escalated into a full-scale humanitarian crisis, marking clear impact materialisation. Food ration cuts and funding shortages have left 85,000 refugees nearly half the camp populations in Kakuma and Kalobeyei without assistance, triggering widespread hunger, protests, and violent clashes with police. As conditions deteriorated, more than 9,300 South Sudanese refugees have returned home since June 2025, many through Nadapal into Eastern Equatoria. The majority are children, now exposed to ambushes, unsafe border conditions, poor sanitation, and heightened risks of gender-based violence (GBV) and disease. Within the camps, worsening socioeconomic conditions have driven a spike in crime, GBV, and early or forced marriages, while malnutrition among children and pregnant or lactating women continues to rise. Water shortages, service interruptions, and dengue fever outbreaks in Dadaab further reflect the strain on essential services. Host communities are increasingly overstretched, facing overcrowding, food insecurity, and limited access to health and shelter, amplifying humanitarian needs for both refugees and hosts.

title: Escalations between loyalists to former President Bashar Al Assad and Sunni armed groups result in internal and cross-border displacement
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale:
There is a high risk of tensions escalating between groups still loyal to the former President and others affiliated with the transitional Government. Resulting clashes in the next months could affect communities along religious lines, particularly conflict between Alawite communities and Sunni groups. The formation of armed groups, such as the Military Council to Liberate Syria, localised in western Syria and led by former Al Assad army commanders, indicates the likelihood of organised resistance against the transitional Government. Conflict dynamics are likely to be localised but could evolve into sectarian clashes in mixed-population areas, such as Homs and parts of Rural Damascus. Road blockages, targeted assassinations, and raids on civilian populations are likely scenarios, considering what already transpired in March 2025: clashes began on 6 March after armed Al Assad loyalists ambushed a security force convoy near Lattakia, killing 13 officers and prompting a harsh military response from the transitional Government’s allied forces. Between 6–8 March, transitional Government security operations targeting Alawite neighbourhoods and villages in Hama, Lattakia, and Tartous killed at least 396 people, predominantly Alawite civilians. Unconfirmed estimates indicate up to 1,500 fatalities during these attacks.
The current sociopolitical dynamics in the country point towards a high probability of an escalation of social tensions along sectarian lines. The dismantling of Al Assad’s security apparatus without a clear reintegration plan, such as restoring former personnel to comparable roles or maintaining their salaries, has deepened a sense of marginalisation among many former President Al Assad loyalists, most of whom are Alawite. Attempts by the new authorities to absorb some of these forces into the new national army have largely been met with suspicion, both from opposition groups — those who previously opposed Al Assad’s regime — and other minority communities, such as Druze and Kurds. These minority communities are concerned about the potential return of oppressive practices, referring both to the military tactics that the Al Assad regime used and to fears that former regime loyalists could regain influence. The latter has the potential to drive imbalances in representation within the new forces, as Kurdish and Druze participation remains limited or symbolic in key command structures.
Minority groups, including the Alawite community, are also concerned that the War Spoils Committee, originally established in 2015 in Idleb to confiscate the properties of Al Assad loyalists, may resume its activities in Damascus and other parts of Syria under the new transitional Government, despite reports that its operations have been dormant and rebranded in 2022 under different names, such as the Properties Committee or Housing Institution. The confiscation of properties will further economically marginalise the Alawite and aggravate tensions. Some reports indicate that confiscations have resumed, though there has been no official announcement that the War Spoils Committee has been re-established. In January 2025, unidentified armed men claiming to be from the General Security Service of the transitional Government ordered an unknown number of Alawite families to evict their homes in Damascus.
Despite the factors contributing to the likelihood of further clashes between Al Assad loyalists and Sunni armed groups, there are efforts aimed at de-escalation. President Ahmed Al Sharaa has condemned the killings of Alawites and pledged to hold all involved accountable, including those within his own ranks. In March, he announced the formation of an independent national committee comprising judges to specifically investigate the events and violations in coastal areas. The committee has also engaged in controversial dialogue with figures from the Al Assad Government, including Fadi Saqr, a former commander of the National Defence Forces accused of abuses against Sunni civilians, as part of broader efforts to engage Alawite communities and prevent renewed violence.
If the investigations are delayed or neglected and the grievances among Alawite communities are not adequately addressed, particularly demands for justice, transparent accountability for the killings, and protection from further reprisal, besides addressing fears of exclusion and collective punishment, this will likely contribute to further violence. Already, the Alawite have found unwelcome a three-month extension beginning in April granted by President Al Sharaa on the deadline for the investigation of the coastal killings, stating concerns of buying time to hide facts. ([ACAPS 22/07/2025](https://www.acaps.org/fileadmin/Data_Product/Main_media/20250722_ACAPS_Syria-_Risk_analysis__July-December_2025__.pdf))

title: The escalation of clashes between Druze and Sunni armed groups leads to displacement and increased needs for food, shelter, water, and healthcare
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale:
A further escalation of clashes between Sunni armed groups and Druze communities is likely, following a sectarian flare-up in late April 2025 and the transitional Government’s failure to contain the security fallout. Escalations may spread across Al Sweida and southern Damascus districts, particularly if Israel’s involvement intensifies or Druze factions become fragmented further.
On 26 April, a fabricated audio recording attributed to a Druze individual insulting the Prophet Muhammad circulated online, prompting enraged Sunni non-state armed groups to attack Druze neighbourhoods near Damascus. Clashes broke out on 28 April in the predominantly Druze districts of Jaramana and Sahnaya in Damascus as local Druze fighters exchanged fire with Sunni gunmen. The fighting spread south to Al Sweida governorate in villages including Al Soura Al Kubra, Ira, and Rasas, killing around 100 people from both sides. The clashes displaced an unknown number of families from some affected areas, likely within the governorate and temporarily.
The transitional Government’s inability to maintain security, coupled with weak control over Sunni armed groups, has emerged as a major trigger for renewed Druze-Sunni clashes. Some of these militias have independently targeted minority communities, including the Druze. Sunni armed groups, whether affiliated with the transitional Government or operating independently, are likely to launch further attacks on Druze-populated areas in Al Sweida and around Damascus, especially along the Damascus–Al Sweida highway and the Al Sweida–Dar’a border.
Sunni armed groups in Syria may target Druze communities for a combination of sectarian and strategic reasons. Some Sunni factions, including former HTS members, have historically viewed the Druze as heretical, leading to attacks, forced conversions, and property seizures justified by extremist ideology. Al Sweida is also important for Sunni armed groups to control because of its strategic location and political symbolism. Geographically, it borders key Sunni-dominated regions such as Dar’a and provides access to smuggling routes into Jordan, making it a vital corridor for the movement of fighters, weapons, and supplies. Politically, asserting control over Al Sweida allows Sunni factions to disrupt any future attempts at Druze autonomy or external support from Druze populations in Lebanon and the Golan Heights.
In response, Druze fighters are expected to retaliate, particularly in the absence of swift and effective intervention by the authorities. Previous government efforts to contain the violence have failed, as affiliated militias have themselves been involved in the clashes, exposing deep operational fragmentation. In April, the Government deployed limited forces and attempted mediation, but divisions within the security apparatus and perceived bias towards Sunni factions weakened its response. This fractured security landscape has intensified mistrust among Druze communities, especially following the mass killings of Alawites by Sunni armed groups in March 2025, an outcome the Druze fear they may also face. As a result, Druze militias have refused to disarm, with no indication that the transitional Government can address its current issue of having weak state control.
Israel will likely deepen its involvement, shifting from air strikes to deploying troops or proxies near the Druze-majority areas under the pretext of protecting them, risking confrontation with the transitional Government. In such cases, fighting could erupt in Al Sweida and surrounding villages, the outskirts of Damascus (Jaramana and Sahnaya), and possibly Quneitra, where the Druze are mostly located. Displacement from Druze-majority and nearby Sunni areas will likely follow, increasing humanitarian needs.
Israel’s interference in the tensions between the Druze and the transitional Government is likely to drive wider confrontations between Druze and Sunni armed groups, especially in the case of further Israeli ground incursions or the direct arming of Druze factions. In the clashes that happened in late April, Israeli drones and jets targeted Sunni armed groups near Sahnaya and bombed sites close to the presidential palace in Damascus. While Israel claimed these were defensive actions in support of the Druze, most Druze leaders have rejected the gesture, fearing it serves Israeli interests in expansion and not theirs. It also portrays them as allies to Israel, an idea that most Druze reject. Syrian officials have condemned the strikes as violations of sovereignty, and activists have accused Israel of using the clashes between the Druze and Sunni armed groups to justify deeper interference and military expansion in southern Syria.
A compounding factor likely to aggravate this conflict and the subsequent humanitarian impact is growing division among the Druze. Some Druze groups, including leaders from the Men of Dignity movement, have engaged with the transitional Government, joined ceasefire talks between Druze and Sunni armed groups, and integrated into local security forces to protect their areas. Others, led by figures such as Sheikh Hikmat Al Hijri, have rejected cooperation, calling the Government ‘terrorists’ and demanding international protection. Some activists in Al Sweida have even called for Druze self-governance over Al Sweida, citing instances in the past when the Druze managed their own affairs independently. So far, no fighting has broken out internally between Druze factions, but tensions are rising. If one side accuses the other of compromising community safety, local clashes are likely to erupt, causing more insecurity in affected areas in southern Syria or some districts in Damascus. Fractures among the Druze community can also allow for foreign interference from Israel or create openings for Sunni armed groups to attack the Druze again, possibly leading to further tensions.
De-escalation between Druze and Sunni armed groups depends on the transitional Government’s ability to control Sunni militias and protect Druze areas. Local ceasefires show that dialogue with Druze leaders can lead to a de-escalation of fighting, avoiding further clashes. That said, these arrangements remain fragile given some opposing Druze factions rejecting deals, local resistance to disarmament, the absence of official investigations into the violence, and the role of external parties such as Israel, whose interventions can contribute to deepening sectarian divisions. ([ACAPS 22/07/2025](https://www.acaps.org/fileadmin/Data_Product/Main_media/20250722_ACAPS_Syria-_Risk_analysis__July-December_2025__.pdf))
hazard_materialisation: This risk has largely materialised. Until 24 November 2025, about 187,000 people remained displaced as a result of clashes and insecurity in Al Sweida governorate. Since the clashes broke out between Druze and Bedouin communities in July, government forces have been struggling to restore safety and security, indicating their weak control over armed groups. ([OCHA 13/11/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/syrian-arab-republic/syrian-arab-republic-humanitarian-response-southern-syria-situation-report-no-3-11-november-2025), [IMC 19/11/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/syrian-arab-republic/sweida-emergency-response-situation-report-u6-november-19-2025))

High protection needs are also reported as a result of localised clashes, movement restrictions, and sporadic security incidents, including explosive ordnance-related casualties. Needs for food continue to be high, driven by shortages of bread given the limited supplies entering the governorate, resulting in the closure of bakeries. Humanitarian aid trucks can enter the governorate, but tensions and sporadic violence along key routes, such as the Damascus–Al Sweida route, often restrict access. These also limit civilian movement and access to essential services. ([OCHA 13/11/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/syrian-arab-republic/syrian-arab-republic-humanitarian-response-southern-syria-situation-report-no-3-11-november-2025), [IMC 19/11/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/syrian-arab-republic/sweida-emergency-response-situation-report-u6-november-19-2025))

title: Further Israeli expansion in southern Syria triggers armed group resistance, displacement, and heightened food insecurity
rationale:
Israel is likely to expand deeper into southern Syria to prevent a potential return of Iran-backed militias, such as Hezbollah, and respond to escalating sectarian violence, particularly near Druze communities, under the pretext of security and humanitarian intervention. This expansion, driven by the transitional Government’s inability to maintain control and provide protection, could result in further displacement and local clashes.
Immediately after the fall of Al Assad’s rule in December 2024, Israel expanded its presence in southern Syria, seizing the demilitarised buffer zone (around 400km²) beyond the Golan Heights and occupying strategic areas in Quneitra, including Tel Al Hara and several border villages. The Israeli Defense Forces (IDF) launched intensive air strikes targeting Syrian and Iranian military infrastructure, significantly weakening local resistance, which included remnants of Syrian army units and Iran-backed militias still active in the area at the time. These moves prompted clashes and displacement, notably from villages such as Al Hameidiyyeh, Rasem Al Rawadi, and Um Batna in Quneitra, with at least 100 Syrian families forcibly displaced by December. Many displaced civilians fled to Damascus or safer towns outside Israeli-held territory.
Israel sees the potential return of Iran-backed militias, especially Hezbollah, as a driver for further expansion in southern Syria, regardless of how likely that return may be. Although many of these forces withdrew after Al Assad’s fall, Israeli officials remain concerned they will regroup in areas near the Golan Heights, such as Quneitra and parts of western Dar’a governorate. The IDF are already positioned just over 20km from Damascus and have declared the presence of any Iranian or Iranian-backed groups a red line, indicating it would trigger immediate air strikes or other military responses to prevent their advancement near Israeli-controlled areas. The transitional Government has condemned the Israeli presence but avoided direct confrontation, focusing instead on internal stability. If Hezbollah attempts to re-establish rocket sites or weapon routes, Israel will likely push deeper into Quneitra or even Dar’a to enforce its buffer zone.
If sectarian attacks escalate near Israeli-held areas, especially against Druze communities, Israel is also likely to expand its presence in Syria under the pretext of protecting the minorities. For example, in April 2025, the IDF conducted air strikes near Damascus, targeting Sunni armed groups accused of attacking Druze civilians in Sahnaya district in the governorate, and subsequently evacuated three wounded Druze individuals to Israeli hospitals. Israel has publicly committed to protecting Syrian Druze. With Sunni and other armed groups subjecting Druze-majority towns to attacks, any assault may prompt a group of Druze leaders to seek Israeli help, especially the ones following Sheikh Hikmat Al Hijri, who is trying to establish stronger relations with Israel. A wider Israeli incursion into Al Sweida may be framed as a humanitarian intervention to protect Druze civilians from sectarian violence or Government-affiliated militias, though most Druze still reject annexation and prefer local autonomy within Syria under the transitional Government.
Another factor triggering Israel’s expansion into southern Syria is the transitional Government’s continued struggle with lack of security. Some non-state armed groups remain active in Quneitra and Dar’a. With some of Al Assad’s Syrian army units fleeing the country and others switching allegiance to the new Government, Israel has stepped in, issuing ultimatums for groups in the Yarmouk Basin to surrender all weapons, submit to home searches, and evacuate their villages or face military action. This has forced many families to evacuate their homes. Israeli officials claim the move is necessary to prevent armed groups from building up near their border. If the transitional Government fails to gain control, Israel is likely to deepen its presence, expanding the buffer zone under the pretext of counterterrorism. So far, the transitional Government has not taken any steps to oppose Israel’s expansion in southern Syria.
The IDF could move far beyond the initial 15km buffer zone towards the Damascus–Al Sweida highway, aiming to secure most of Quneitra and Dar’a and parts of Al Sweida. Syrian factions, including armed groups affiliated with the transitional Government, might try to stop the advance, though their capacity to pose a sustained military threat remains limited owing to fragmentation, resource constraints, and a lack of advanced weaponry. There is also a low to medium likelihood of Iran and Hezbollah reopening fronts in Lebanon or southern Syria to slow Israeli gains. The probability of large-scale retaliation remains moderate to low, and isolated attacks or proxy activity are more likely.
The continued absence of the transitional Government in these areas, its inability to counter Israeli expansion, and failure to protect civilians are likely to fuel further tensions and protests similar to the ones that erupted in Al Sweida in April 2025 against Israel and the Government’s failure to protect civilians. Between 8 December 2024 and 12 June 2025, Israeli attacks killed at least 22 civilians in Al Sweida, Dar’a, Quneitra, and Rural Damascus. ([ACAPS 22/07/2025](https://www.acaps.org/fileadmin/Data_Product/Main_media/20250722_ACAPS_Syria-_Risk_analysis__July-December_2025__.pdf))
hazard_materialisation: The hazard partially materialised. Israel continued to expand and consolidate its military presence in southern Syria through repeated ground incursions, arrests, checkpoints, civilian property destruction, and movement restrictions, particularly across Quneitra and western Dar’a governorates. Israeli forces established additional military positions and normalised near-daily operations inside Syrian territory, while protests against the continued military presence increased from June–July 2026, reflecting growing civilian resentment. Israel also continued to justify its operations on security grounds and the protection of Druze communities. That said, the risk overestimated the likelihood that Israeli expansion would trigger sustained armed resistance by Syrian factions or Iran-backed groups. Instead, opposition remained largely limited to local protests and isolated confrontations, while the transitional Government continued to avoid direct military confrontation with Israel. Likewise, Israeli operations did not expand into the broader territorial advance towards As Sweida or the Damascus–As Sweida highway suggested in the risk.
impact_materialisation_description:
The expected humanitarian impacts partially materialised. Continued Israeli incursions displaced additional households, damaged homes, roads, water infrastructure, and agricultural land, and restricted civilian access to farmland and essential services in affected communities, increasing humanitarian needs and disrupting livelihoods.

Displacement directly attributable to Israeli military operations in southern Syria remained fragmented and underreported. The most documented case of permanent displacement occurred in Al Hamidiyah, Quneitra, where Israel forcibly expelled 12 families by demolishing 16 homes to construct a military base in the months after December 2024. Incident-specific figures point to larger but temporary movements; an Israeli incursion in Beit Jinn, Rural Damascus, in November 2025 temporarily displaced approximately 1,500 people, while the Israeli shelling of Abdin village in western Dar’a on 29 June 2026 caused around 2,000 residents to flee to neighbouring villages, most of whom returned shortly after.

Humanitarian responders also reported growing protection concerns linked to arrests, movement restrictions, and repeated military operations in Quneitra and Dar’a. That said, the anticipated scale of displacement did not materialise. There was no evidence of a large-scale offensive comparable to the 2018 Dar’a campaign or significant cross-border displacement into Jordan.

title: A prolonged Syria–Lebanon border conflict results in displacement and increases shelter and livelihood needs
rationale:
The Syria–Lebanon border remains a key smuggling corridor for fuel, drugs (especially Captagon), and weapons, primarily from Syria to Lebanon, often facilitated by networks linked to Hezbollah and Iran-backed militias. After Al Assad’s fall, Syria’s transitional Government’s forces launched an anti-smuggling campaign in early 2025, targeting routes used by Hezbollah-linked clans near Al Qasr village on the Lebanese side of the border. Armed networks, such as the Jaafar clan (of Lebanon), resisted violently, ambushing Syrian patrols and firing anti-tank rockets. These confrontations escalated into clashes in March near Al Qasr.
Without clear coordination between Lebanese and Syrian authorities, both aiming to stop smuggling, efforts to dismantle these networks will likely trigger more cross-border skirmishes, especially in areas where smuggling remains a main source of income and power for local armed groups.
On 16 March 2025, clashes broke out along the Syria–Lebanon border after transitional Government soldiers crossed into Lebanon and were shot by local Lebanese clans. Syria’s transitional Government accused Hezbollah of abducting and executing three of its soldiers, which Hezbollah denied. In response, Syrian troops shelled Lebanese border villages, killing civilians and triggering counterfire from local clans and the Lebanese Army. The two days of fighting killed at least ten people, including a 15-year-old boy, and wounded over 50 in Al Qasr. The two Governments reached a ceasefire on 17 March, ending the clashes.
Areas including Al Qasr have served as hubs for Iranian weapon transfers, protected by clan networks aligned with Hezbollah. Another factor driving tensions between Syria and Lebanon is, in fact, Hezbollah’s presence along Lebanon’s northeast border and its ties to local Shia clans and longstanding smuggling routes from Syria. Syria’s new transitional Government sees these ties as a security threat and has targeted Shia-populated border zones, shelling villages and expelling Lebanese Shia families. Hezbollah has avoided direct clashes with Syria’s transitional Government so far, but tensions have been rising between the two parties and within Lebanon, between Hezbollah and the Lebanese Government. When Lebanese forces seized Hezbollah weapons in April, local supporters of the party and armed groups accused the Lebanese army of betraying them for cooperating with Syria.
If crackdowns on smuggling continue and Hezbollah and drug-smuggling criminal groups see their supply routes further threatened, localised armed confrontations along the border also have the potential to turn into broader fighting. Syrian forces already advanced up to 5–7km into Lebanese territory around Al Qasr in March to dismantle smuggling routes, and further incursions to similarly shallow depths — meaning within the 5–7km border zone — remain possible, though recent diplomatic talks between the Governments of Lebanon and Syria in April and the creation of a joint border committee may reduce the likelihood of a sustained escalation. The committee, established as part of a bilateral border agreement, is a ministerial-level body tasked with coordinating border management, preventing unauthorised crossings, and overseeing dispute resolution in sensitive areas.
Although Syrian forces have imposed military control over the border with Lebanon, challenges such as difficult terrain, Hezbollah’s presence, and some southern clans’ reliance on smuggling continue to threaten lasting border security. These factors may enable smuggling networks to regroup, casting doubt on Syria’s capacity for sustained and effective border monitoring. Hezbollah could respond militarily to any advance of Syrian troops, not only to defend strategic smuggling routes that sustain its operations but also to assert its role as a protector of Lebanese sovereignty and maintain influence in border areas with high Shia presence. That said, considering the conflict between Hezbollah and Israel between October 2023 and November 2024, which significantly weakened Hezbollah’s military capacity, the likelihood of its direct engagement remains between medium to low.
Given its limited capacity and history of constrained responses, including during recent Israeli operations, the Lebanese Army is unlikely to play a decisive role but may be drawn into localised clashes. On the other hand, Syrian Sunni armed groups could exploit the instability to target Lebanese and Syrian Shia communities in border areas, driven by sectarian tensions and perceptions of Hezbollah’s alignment with Al Assad’s rule, further escalating the violence. Although the likelihood of escalating tensions and an advance by the new Syrian army remains moderate, the consequences could include a prolonged border conflict, mass displacement, and rising casualties on both sides. [(ACAPS 22/07/2025)](https://www.acaps.org/fileadmin/Data_Product/Main_media/20250722_ACAPS_Syria-_Risk_analysis__July-December_2025__.pdf))

title: Severe shortage of services triggers unrest and breakout attempts in Al Hol and Al Roj camps
rationale:
If security in Al Hol and Al Roj camps collapses due to mass rioting or breakouts, ISIS-affiliated IDPs are likely to escape, regroup, and rejoin IS cells, potentially sparking renewed insurgencies in both Syria and Iraq. Unlike typical displacement sites, Al Hol and Al Roj function as detention facilities housing individuals with suspected IS ties, including non-Syrians and their families, making the risk of escape a security concern rather than a humanitarian one. As of April 2024, Al Hol hosts 42,000 people, and as of December 2024 Al Roj hosts over 2,600 people. As of early April, around 1,500 international troops remain in Syria, some of whom are tasked with preventing an IS resurgence; large-scale escapes could prompt renewed military operations in Syria. Iraqi officials have repeatedly warned that instability in Al Hol poses a direct threat to their internal security, as escaped IS members may attempt to cross into Iraq. Compounding this risk, a recent US funding freeze has weakened camp management, including WASH services, and could create further security vacuums that IS may exploit.
In January 2025, President Trump’s administration ordered a temporary freeze on nearly all US foreign aid, including humanitarian assistance. This affected funding to support humanitarian programmes and aid delivery in northeastern Syria. Aid and service delivery in Al Hol camp and Al Roj camp, hosting people displaced from areas previously under the control of the IS in Syria, had relied heavily on USAID support. In 2024, the United States spent over 1.2 billion US dollars on humanitarian aid in Syria and the Middle East, far more than any other donor. The US contributed with 24% of the total funding for Syria in 2024 within the coordinated response plan, followed by Germany which contributed with almost 14%. The United States contributions to Al Hol operations were ten times larger than those of the next largest funder.
Even with a short-term waiver for life-saving aid, the funding pause has already disrupted some humanitarian services. Humanitarian workers report that once USAID contracts were frozen, agencies delivering fuel, food and water became unsure how to proceed. The US-funded contractor Blumont, responsible for camp management at Al Hol and Al Roj, halted its activities on 24 January and pulled out all personnel, including security staff. This led to immediate gaps in essential operations of water trucking, sanitation, food distributions, and education. As the temporary measures used to manage the funding cuts crisis, such as using emergency funds and relying on other NGOs, are almost depleting, conditions in the camps are expected to worsen further. If US funding remains frozen, Al Hol and Al Roj will face acute shortages of food, fuel, and medicine, and the threat of disease which is likely to result in civil unrest and increase insecurity.
Overcrowding and poor sanitation have already fuelled disease. For example, a cholera outbreak impacted Al Hol camp in late 2024. The already poor WASH infrastructure in the camps, aggravated by the disruption of services due to the US funding freeze, is likely to trigger mass rioting and breakout attempts. Escapes are already common, especially from Al Hol camp, where escapes are reported every week. Most of those who escape are females and children of foreign nationalities.
On 26 May, the transitional Government and Kurdish authorities reached an agreement on a mechanism to safely evacuate Syrian families from Al Hol camp to Damascus. This measure is likely to ease pressure on camp services and reduce the likelihood of mass riots or breakout attempts by the camp’s IDPs. However, as of 12 June, it remains unclear how many people will be evacuated or whether the process has already begun. As of 27 May, approximately 200 Syrian IDPs were being prepared for return from Al Hol to Aleppo governorate. Additionally, 800 Iraqi IDPs were transferred from Al Hol to Al Jada’a camp in Mosul governorate, northern Iraq on 31 May. It is likely that those returns are not part of the new agreement between the transitional Government and the Kurdish authorities.([ECHO 19/06/2024](https://reliefweb.int/report/syrian-arab-republic/syria-historic-drought-impacting-food-security-dg-echo-un-ocha-fao-wfp-echo-daily-flash-19-june-2025), [FAO accessed12/09/2025](https://openknowledge.fao.org/items/bf52f354-c8f3-4f3f-9367-4d5347016c7b), [UNICEF accessed 12/09/2025](https://www.unicef.org/syria/situation-children-syria), [CSIC accessed 12/09/2025](https://features.csis.org/the-future-of-the-Euphrates-River/), [Ul 03/05/2025](https://ultrasyria.ultrasawt.com))
hazard_materialisation: The risk has largely materialised, as Syrian officials had reported a mass escape of families and relatives of suspected Islamic State fighters by 26 February. The main trigger for the mass escape was the withdrawal of Syrian Democratic Forces, unlike what the risk raised by ACAPS suggested, which was that breakouts from the camp would stem from service shortages following US funding cuts. Similar to what the risk suggested, however, many camp residents continued to be transferred to Aleppo governorate in Syria, and the Iraqi residents have likely been returned to Iraq. ([AJ 26/02/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/2/26/syria-confirms-mass-escape-from-camp-housing-relatives-of-isil-fighters#:~:text=News%7CISIL/ISIS-,Syria%20confirms%20'mass%20escape'%20from%20camp%20housing%20relatives%20of%20ISIL,SDF's%20withdrawal%20from%20the%20camp.&text=A%20Syrian%20official%20has%20confirmed,11%2Dmile))

title: Water scarcity, especially in northeast and northwest Syria result in livelihoods and services’ disruptions, reduced food production and protests
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale:
As of February 2025, about 13.6 million Syrians lack access to safe water and sanitation. Conflict since 2011 has damaged water infrastructure, resulting in a 40% reduction in the drinking water supply as of 2021. Almost half of the water systems no longer function reliably, forcing many to rely on tankers or unsafe wells. Ongoing electricity and fuel shortages have crippled water pumps and treatment plants, exacerbating water rationing and existing sanitation problems and driving disease outbreaks. 
Syria and the region experienced an exceptionally dry winter and spring in 2024/2025, with significantly below-average rainfall and higher temperatures. In April 2025, water levels in Lake Euphrates Dam dropped to about six meters, which is five meters below the normal level.
Upstream water retention and weaponisation of water are also drivers of water scarcity in Syria. Türkiye has sharply reduced the Euphrates’ waters flow into Syria by restricting releases from upstream dams, such as the Atatürk Dam, often to around 200 cubic meters per second, well below the 500 cubic meters per second agreed in bilateral treaties. It has also used dam releases as political leverage and targeted key water infrastructure like the Alouk station in Al Hasakah in August 2024 and October 2023, disrupting access to water for more than a million people. Similarly, Israel’s occupation of the Golan Heights since 1981 and control over the Yarmouk basin and Unity (Al Wahda) dam in December 2024 have cut Syria off from its southern water sources. Communities, especially agricultural, living in southern Syria are likely to experience the impact of the loss of these water sources throughout 2025.
The lean season in Syria typically runs from June to September. In 2025, it will likely be one of the driest since 1989. April forecasts showed poor soil moisture and low reservoir levels heading into summer. As rainfall was far below average during the October–April season, water scarcity will likely intensify through June to September. Water levels are likely to continue to decrease in 2025, as projections indicate that by 2050, Syria’s water supply will decrease by 20%.
Water-related tensions have driven protests and localised disputes before, and are likely to drive further protests and disputes in 2025. In June 2024, water shortages and electricity cuts led to localised protests in Al Hasakeh. In February 2024, residents in Deir ez-Zor protested over lack of drinking water and accused local officials of corruption. In July 2022, displaced people in several camps in north Idlib protested water shortages, while water service providers went on a strike to protest an international organisation's decision to reduce water supplies.
Northeast and Northwest Syria, particularly Al Hasakeh, Al Raqqa, Idlib, and rural Aleppo, are likely hotspots for water-related tensions during the 2025 lean season. People’s livelihoods in these areas are already the most impacted by water scarcity, and they have limited alternative sources. If shortages persist, it is likely that people will protest at wells or water trucks, attempt to blockade water pipelines, or engage in local skirmishes over water resources. For example, communities might block a contested pump station or forcibly redirect tanker convoys. ([ECHO 19/06/2024](https://reliefweb.int/report/syrian-arab-republic/syria-historic-drought-impacting-food-security-dg-echo-un-ocha-fao-wfp-echo-daily-flash-19-june-2025), [FAO accessed12/09/2025](https://openknowledge.fao.org/items/bf52f354-c8f3-4f3f-9367-4d5347016c7b), [UNICEF accessed 12/09/2025](https://www.unicef.org/syria/situation-children-syria), [CSIC accessed 12/09/2025](https://features.csis.org/the-future-of-the-Euphrates-River/), [Ul 03/05/2025](https://ultrasyria.ultrasawt.com))

title: Tension over limited resources leads to localised clashes in Hodh Ech Chargui wilaya
rationale:
As of July 2025, pressure over limited resources continues to increase, especially in Hodh Ech Chargui wilaya, where the number of Malian refugees continues to increase, while drought and seasonal dry conditions continue in depletion of water and grazing resources, which may trigger tensions and localized clashes. 
The southeastern Hodh Chargui wilaya, which borders Mali, now hosts over 160,000 Malian refugees as of 30 June 2025, compromising over 25.5% of the total population of the wilaya, up from 19% in 2024. The refugee-to-host population ratio in some areas exceeds 1:4, straining access to local sources of water, fuel wood, and grazing land. Competition for scarce water, land, and grazing resources is intensifying between refugees, local communities, and Mauritanian returnees, who were previously displaced from Mali due to insecurity and violence. Localised tensions over access to farmland and grazing areas are often reported and is likely, as was the case in 2022 following a large influx of Malian refugees into Mauritania. Simultaneously, recurring climate shocks such as prolonged droughts, which have affected the country for several decades, and floods in 2024, which displaced 1,125 people and caused damage to agriculture and grazing areas, have weakened rural livelihoods, especially in agropastoral areas where over 60% of the population depends on rain-fed agriculture and livestock.
If refugee flows from Mali continue or host resources become further depleted, social cohesion could be further disrupted, triggering localised clashes between communities over land, water, and grazing access. Departments such as Bassikounou, Fassala, and Amourj, that host the highest Malian refugees population and where land tenure is contested between returnees and local families, are likely to report localised clashes. title: Escalating tensions around universal suffrage in Somalia heightens conflict and instability ahead of the 2026 elections
rationale:
Somalia is transitioning from a clan-based indirect electoral system to universal suffrage for the 2026 elections, marking the first attempt in over 50 years to hold nationwide one-person-one-vote polls. In August 2025, the Federal Government and opposition leaders signed an agreement establishing the framework for parliament members to be directly elected. The agreement has also deepened rifts within the main opposition coalition, the Forum for National Salvation, with former president Sharif Sheikh Ahmed insisting that the prevailing insecurity makes the implementation of such extensive electoral reforms unfeasible.
While representing democratic progress, this shift is occurring in a fragile political environment marked by unresolved disputes between the Federal Government and federal member states (FMSes). Puntland has rejected the constitutional reforms underpinning universal suffrage, warning of potential violence. Jubaland state has also experienced armed clashes over disputed electoral processes in recent years.
As voter registration rolls out and constituency boundaries are drawn, clan grievances and FMS–Federal Government tensions are likely to intensify. This political disunity, characterised by persistent rivalries and potential boycotts from opposition and states such as Puntland and Jubaland, will impede unified counterterrorism efforts, consequently increasing overall insecurity and humanitarian needs. Regions and dominant clans feeling marginalised may resist the reforms politically or militarily, sparking localised violence as they seek to assert control. If the elections are ultimately delayed, boycotted, or politically contested, the resulting legitimacy crisis could also escalate into violent clashes or a governance breakdown. Specifically, the collapse of the federal electoral process risks reigniting widespread clan conflicts and political violence.
Simultaneously, Al Shabaab is poised to exploit this instability. Leveraging an intensification of offensives and territorial gains expected in 2025, the group will target voter registration sites, polling centres, and civilians. This will not only undermine electoral credibility but also worsen the security environment ahead of elections and disrupt critical humanitarian access. These conflict dynamics will be severely multiplied by climate shocks and persistent food insecurity, further straining community resources and worsening the complex security and humanitarian landscape. ([Africanews 26/08/2025](https://www.africanews.com/2025/08/26/somalias-president-and-opposition-leaders-reach-historic-election-agreement/), [Reuters 08/08/2024](https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/somalias-cabinet-approves-bill-universal-suffrage-2024-08-08/?), [The Guardian 05/04/2024](https://www.theguardian.com/global-development/2024/apr/05/fears-violence-somalia-constitution?), [RVI accessed 07/10/2025](https://riftvalley.net/publication/prospects-for-somalias-transition-from-clan-based-politics-to-multipartyism-in-the-2026-election/))
hazard_materialisation: The hazard materialised in August as political tensions between the Federal Government and South West state escalated into armed confrontation in Baidoa city in South West state. On 17 August 2026, federal forces and militias aligned with former South West state president Abdiaziz Laftagareen fought in and around the city, marking a major escalation in the political dispute identified by the risk. ([Reuters 17/08/2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/somalia-federal-troops-armed-opposition-clash-baidoa-city-2026-08-17/), [MSF 17/08/2026](https://prezly.msf.org.uk/statement-clashes-in-baidoa-and-wounded-arriving-at-msf-supported-hospital))
impact_materialisation_description: The anticipated humanitarian impacts materialised in August 2026 as the political confrontation in Baidoa city, Bay region, South West state, caused civilian casualties and disrupted security in a major displacement hub. The 17 August fighting killed four people and wounded 71, including women and children, who are being treated at Bay Regional Hospital. Casualties are expected to rise, while residents report damage to homes and buildings. The violence demonstrates the anticipated civilian protection and health consequences of political confrontation. ([Reuters 17/08/2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/somalia-federal-troops-armed-opposition-clash-baidoa-city-2026-08-17/), [AJ 17/08/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/17/somali-army-clashes-with-rebel-forces-for-control-of-key-city-baidoa), [MSF 17/08/2026](https://prezly.msf.org.uk/statement-clashes-in-baidoa-and-wounded-arriving-at-msf-supported-hospital))

title: Rising water scarcity in Iran leads to a deterioration in health, food security, and livelihood needs
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale:
Iran’s current water crisis is expected to worsen, with warnings that Tehran could face severe water shortages affecting large parts of the city by October 2025 if water consumption is not drastically reduced. The country has endured a five-year drought, and reservoirs supplying major cities have fallen to their lowest levels in a century. In Tehran, key reservoirs dropped to roughly 14% capacity during peak heat periods, causing widespread water service cuts and outages lasting 12–18 hours in some districts.
Critically low reservoir levels have also hampered hydroelectric power generation, aggravating electricity shortages already driven by fuel constraints and extreme heat. Between June–August, temperatures exceeding 50° C in provinces including Khuzestan, Sistan-Baluchestan, and Yazd led to power and water outages disrupting cooling systems, medical facilities, and water pumping networks. Hospitals report difficulties in maintaining refrigeration for medicines and stable operations during rolling blackouts. At the same time, heat-related mortality has spiked among vulnerable populations, particularly older and displaced people, highlighting severe strain on public health infrastructure. Waterborne disease outbreaks are becoming increasingly likely as water quality deteriorates and sanitation systems falter.
As water scarcity and livelihood pressures intensify, affected populations are likely to seek opportunities in neighbouring countries, including Afghanistan, Iraq, Pakistan, and Türkiye. Political tensions and security concerns may increase irregular migration flows, further aggravating humanitarian needs for displaced people.
Recurrent protests across Fars, Isfahan, and Khuzestan over water and electricity shortages also signal eroding public patience and raise the risk of broader civil unrest amid mounting climate pressures and governance challenges.
([Stimpson 26/03/2025](https://www.stimson.org/2025/no-easy-solutions-for-irans-water-shortages-and-power-outages/), [DW 19/06/2024](https://www.dw.com/en/irans-water-crisis-leads-to-alarming-ground-collapse/a-69405927), [Middle East 18/04/2025](https://middleeast.observer/iran/article/4073/ ), [NCRI 13/08/2025](https://www.ncr-iran.org/en/news/economy/why-iran-is-running-out-of-water-power-and-patience/), [KUNC 17/08/2025](https://www.kunc.org/2025-08-17/iranian-officials-warn-tehran-could-run-out-of-water-in-weeks-amidst-massive-drought),  [Thomson Reuters 17/08/2025](https://www.context.news/climate-risks/opinion/irans-water-crisis-is-driven-by-bad-policies-but-tech-can-help))
hazard_materialisation: The anticipated deterioration in water availability materialised in August 2026 as prolonged drought further depleted already-low water reserves, while conflict-related damage to water infrastructure compounded local supply constraints. By 23 August, storage in Tehran’s five main reservoirs had fallen to 26%, down from around 30% at the beginning of summer and approximately 220 million m³ below the ideal level. Tehran is experiencing its sixth consecutive drought year, with rainfall below 175mm compared with around 280mm needed to restore water conditions. Separately, several villages on Qeshm Island experienced prolonged interruptions to piped water after US strikes damaged desalination infrastructure, demonstrating water supply disruption through environmental and infrastructure-related pathways. ([AA 23/08/2026](https://www.aa.com.tr/fa/%D8%A7%DB%8C%D8%B1%D8%A7%D9%86/%D8%B0%D8%AE%D8%A7%DB%8C%D8%B1-%D8%B3%D8%AF%D9%87%D8%A7%DB%8C-%D8%AA%D9%87%D8%B1%D8%A7%D9%86-%DA%A9%D8%A7%D9%87%D8%B4-%DB%8C%D8%A7%D9%81%D8%AA/4035148), [Iran Wire 04/08/2026](https://iranwire.com/en/news/155841-qeshm-villages-suffer-four-month-water-cut/), [AA 23/08/2026](https://www.aa.com.tr/tr/dunya/tahrandaki-barajlarin-doluluk-orani-yuzde-26ya-geriledi/4035073)).
impact_materialisation_description: The expected humanitarian impact materialised through reduced access to safe drinking water and increased WASH needs. Water shortages have increasingly affected access to safe drinking water, sanitation, hygiene, and livelihoods across Iran. In Hormozgan governorate, damage to the Bunji desalination plant on 18 July disrupted water supplies to at least 20 villages, affecting approximately 10,000 people. Prolonged disruptions are likely to increase reliance on unsafe water sources and household spending on water trucking, heightening public health and protection risks. Nationally, around 35 million people experienced water shortages in May, while critically low reservoirs and drought are increasing pressure on agricultural production. Reduced water availability and potential crop losses of 25–30% are likely to further undermine food security and rural livelihoods. ([Al Sharq 18/07/2026](https://asharq.com/sub-live/politics/60056/%D8%A5%D9%8A%D8%B1%D8%A7%D9%86-%D8%A7%D9%86%D9%82%D8%B7%D8%A7%D8%B9-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%85%D9%8A%D8%A7%D9%87-%D8%B9%D9%86-20-%D9%82%D8%B1%D9%8A%D8%A9-%D8%A8%D8%B9%D8%AF-%D9%87%D8%AC%D9%88%D9%85-%D8%A3%D9%85%D9%8A%D8%B1%D9%83%D9%8A-%D8%A3%D8%B5%D8%A7%D8%A8-%D9%85%D8%AD%D8%B7%D8%A9-%D8%AA%D8%AD%D9%84%D9%8A%D8%A9-%D8%AC%D9%86%D9%88%D8%A8-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A8%D9%84%D8%A7%D8%AF), [Iran Intl 11/05/2026](https://www.iranintl.com/en/202605111643), [Iran Intl 03/05/2026](https://www.iranintl.com/en/202605035394))

Trigger ID: R1008 - T0527
Title: Prolonged Drought and Heatwaves
Description: 
Iran’s worsening water crisis is being driven by prolonged drought and intensifying heatwaves, which have sharply reduced rainfall, surface water, and groundwater reserves. Between October 2024 and March 2025, precipitation declined by 41% below long-term averages and 21% compared to the previous year, severely limiting inflows into dams and reservoirs.
The deficit now affects 30 of 31 provinces, with the harshest shortfalls recorded in Hormozgan (–75.9%), Sistan-Baluchestan (–75.4%), and East Azerbaijan (–60%). Record-breaking heat has accelerated evaporation, compounding the depletion of already scarce supplies. In Tehran, key reservoirs, Latian, Lar, Mamloo, and Amir Kabir, have dropped to just 5–12% capacity, with the Lar dam nearly empty, threatening water security and essential urban services.
The combined effects of persistent drought, extreme heat, and excessive groundwater extraction have disrupted Iran’s hydrological balance, leading to land subsidence, reduced agricultural output, and growing food insecurity. These climatic pressures are central triggers of Iran’s water crisis, exacerbating structural weaknesses in governance, infrastructure, and livelihoods.

Title: Climate Change Amplification
Description: 
Climate change is a major amplifier of Iran’s water crisis, intensifying droughts, heatwaves, and rainfall variability across much of the country. Rising temperatures have accelerated evaporation and reduced snowpack in key mountain ranges, diminishing surface runoff that feeds rivers and reservoirs. Over the past two decades, Iran’s average temperature has increased by more than 1.5°C, with extreme heat events becoming longer and more frequent.
This climatic shift has disrupted traditional rainfall cycles, concentrating precipitation into shorter, more intense bursts that fail to replenish groundwater or sustain agriculture. As a result, 30 of 31 provinces now face chronic water stress, with southern and central regions, such as Khuzestan, Yazd, and Sistan-Baluchestan, experiencing the most severe shortages.
Higher temperatures also drive surging demand for irrigation and domestic consumption, compounding existing overuse of groundwater and depletion of reservoirs. The resulting imbalance has caused widespread subsidence, declining crop yields, and rural displacement.

title: Consecutive below-average rains amid expected La Niña conditions in northern and central Somalia deepen drought Impacts
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale:
A below-average Deyr season (October–December), the third consecutive poor rainy season in northern and central areas, is forecast, at the same time that the probability of La Niña conditions is projected to reach around 60%. This climatic development is expected to reduce rainfall across much of Somalia, prolonging dry conditions and intensifying the effects of several consecutive below-average rainfall seasons. River levels in the Shabelle and Juba River Basins are likely to drop further, increasing water scarcity in riverine and agropastoral zones. Reduced rainfall coupled with rising temperatures will accelerate crop and livestock losses, placing rural livelihoods under severe strain.
In key food-producing regions, such as Bakool, Bay, and Lower Shabelle, maize and groundnut yields have already declined by up to 40% during previous drought years. Many of these areas have shifted from being net exporters to net consumers of basic staples. Declining soil fertility and shrinking pasture resources are expected to raise livestock mortality rates significantly, particularly in Galgaduud, Gedo, and Togdheer. This will erode household incomes and undermine a critical source of national exports.
The deterioration of water infrastructure is a pressing concern. Extended dry periods have reduced groundwater recharge and increased salinity, especially in coastal and riverine areas, making many sources unsafe for consumption and raising health risks. Access to safe water and functional health services continues to diminish, with approximately 40 primary healthcare facilities and 16 mobile health teams closing across 21 districts. Water contamination and displacement have contributed to favourable conditions for disease outbreaks, with more than 6,550 cases of cholera and acute watery diarrhoea reported between January–July.
The compounded impacts of failed rains, collapsing rural livelihoods, and disruptions to basic services are expected to heighten food insecurity and trigger further displacement, particularly in Bakool, Bay, Galgaduud, Gedo, and parts of Mudug and Lower Shabelle. Resource scarcity will likely fuel localised tensions and competition over water and grazing areas, especially between pastoralist and farming communities as well as among ethnic clans. Armed group activity is also expected to intensify, with Al Shabaab likely exploiting the drought to strengthen territorial control. Tactics may include imposing informal taxes on herders and traders, restricting access to water points and interfering with humanitarian aid delivery to consolidate influence. ([OCHA 21/09/2025] (https://www.unocha.org/publications/report/somalia/somalia-monthly-humanitarian-update-august-2025), [OCHA 05/08/2025] (https://www.unocha.org/publications/report/somalia/somalia-drought-conditions-central-and-northern-regions-flash-update-no1-5-august-2025) [ICPAC 26/08/2025] (https://www.icpac.net/news/below-normal-rains-and-warmer-than-usual-conditions-are-expected-over-most-parts-of-the-greater-horn-of-africa/))
hazard_materialisation: The climate hazard partially materialised, although not through the initially anticipated La Niña mechanism. Instead of La Niña-driven below-average Deyr rainfall, Somalia experienced a continuation of drought conditions following failed 2025 Deyr rains and an unusually harsh Jilaal season. By early 2026, drought conditions had intensified, with forecasts indicating delayed and uneven recovery during the 2026 Gu season. The shift towards El Niño later in 2026 changed the expected hazard profile from prolonged drought to a potential drought-to-flood transition, particularly in the Juba and Shabelle River Basins.
impact_materialisation_description: The anticipated humanitarian impacts materialised, as prolonged drought severely affected livelihoods, food security, water availability, and displacement patterns. In January 2026, drought affected an estimated 4.61 million people, with at least 120,000 displaced between September–December 2025. More than 170 boreholes and shallow wells were reported non-functional, while drought conditions contributed to widespread Crisis (IPC Phase 3) and Emergency (IPC Phase 4) food insecurity, with some areas at risk of Catastrophe (IPC Phase 5). Livestock losses, reduced agricultural production, water shortages, and displacement increased humanitarian needs, particularly in central and southern Somalia.

title: US military build-up in the Caribbean triggers internal destabilisation in Venezuela and heightens humanitarian needs
rationale:
The current US military presence in the Caribbean marks the largest deployment in the region in decades, involving multiple strikes against vessels suspected of drug smuggling. This build-up has significantly heightened tensions with Venezuela, which perceives the presence as a direct threat and a prelude to regime change, prompting increased military mobilisation. Opposition groups are likely to interpret these developments as signals of external support or possible military intervention, potentially emboldening them to escalate activities such as strikes, protests, and sabotage. Such actions risk weakening state control and destabilising the Government.
Should opposition momentum grow and fractures emerge within the Nicolás Maduro regime’s internal cohesion, Venezuela could rapidly destabilise without a coordinated transition plan or sustained international engagement. This instability might create power vacuums, especially in regions with limited government presence. Non-state armed groups (NSAGs) and criminal networks could exploit this uncertainty to expand territorial control, particularly in economically strategic zones such as Bolívar state, known for its gold reserves, and the Orinoco Oil Belt, the centre of oil extraction. Civilians in these areas would face severe consequences, including increased violence, targeted attacks, forced displacement, and restricted movement.
At the same time, US antitrafficking campaigns disrupting Caribbean routes for gold, oil, and narcotics will aggravate the crisis by further destabilising the local economy. The intensification of political and economic instability may trigger new waves of displacement, pushing thousands to seek refuge in neighbouring countries including Brazil, Colombia, and Ecuador. These countries, already hosting millions of Venezuelan refugees, will face increased pressure on their humanitarian and basic service systems. The US military operation against Venezuela — designated Operation Absolute Resolve — was carried out on 3 January 2026 by elements of the Delta Force, US Air Force, and US Navy. The operation culminated in the capture of Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores at a safe house in the Venezuelan capital, Caracas, where both were apprehended while asleep. Maduro and Flores were subsequently transferred to New York, where they are currently facing narco-trafficking charges.

title: Escalating armed conflict during the December 2025 election in Myanmar heightens protection risks
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale: The 28 December 2025 election date creates an urgency for the military to assert control by securing contested territories, which is likely to intensify military operations in these areas. The junta’s efforts to establish polling stations in opposition-held regions have already sparked armed clashes, with the military employing overwhelming force to enforce electoral control. Armed opposition groups have openly declared their intent to prevent elections in areas under their control, setting the stage for direct confrontations with military forces attempting to set up polling stations. The junta’s deployment of troops to these contested zones will lead to further armed conflict. This volatile situation will result in increased civilian casualties, mass displacement, and widespread damage to infrastructure, particularly in regions with significant presence of ethnic armed organisations and anti-junta factions. Magway, Mandalay, and Sagaing regions, which experience the most frequent military air strikes across the country, are likely to see further displacement and infrastructure destruction. Intimidation tactics, unlawful detentions, and retaliatory violence by all parties involved will also worsen protection risks and significantly impede humanitarian relief efforts. ([Asian Confluence accessed 09/10/2025](https://www.asianconfluence.org/publication-details-full/myanmar-s-2025-elections-prospects-risks-and-policy-implications), [BBC 18/08/2025](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cvg3pp4n952o), [AA 16/09/2025](https://www.aa.com.tr/en/asia-pacific/no-elections-in-dozens-of-constituencies-during-myanmars-december-polls/3689652), [ICG 18/07/2025](https://www.crisisgroup.org/asia/south-east-asia/myanmar/b184-myanmars-dangerous-drift-conflict-elections-and-looming-regional-detente))
hazard_materialisation: Airstrikes in contested areas increased after the election date was announced, with attacks intended to regain control of areas where voting was scheduled. On election day in December 2025, junta forces continued air and artillery attacks even as polling stations opened in Sagaing, while resistance groups carried out attacks in Mandalay and Myawaddy. At least 170 civilians were killed in around 408 military aerial attacks during the voting period between December 2025 and January 2026. Detentions under the Election Protection Law and retaliatory violence compounded protection concerns but not to the levels suggested in this risk.
