title: Intensified territorial disputes among armed groups over illegal mining corridors in southern Bolívar lead to mass displacement and confinement
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale:
Territorial disputes between non-state armed groups (NSAGs) over the control of strategic corridors and illegal mining activities in southern Bolívar have intensified dramatically since 2023, escalating humanitarian needs. Historically, the National Liberation Army (ELN) maintained territorial control and governance throughout southern Bolívar. The arrival, however, of competing NSAGs – including the Gaitanist Self-Defence Forces of Colombia (AGC), Comandos de la Frontera, dissident groups of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, and others – has fractured this control. This violent competition has triggered frequent armed confrontations, targeted attacks against civilians, population displacement, and confinement, creating acute protection risks.
Conflict dynamics have steadily intensified over the past years. In Bolívar, mass displacements have become increasingly frequent. The number quadrupled from three incidents in 2023 to 16 in 2024, with 12 additional conflict-related emergencies recorded by mid-2025. All these events were in municipalities surrounding the Serranía de San Lucas, a strategic corridor at the centre of territorial disputes. By 8 August 2025, around 13,000 people were displaced, confined, or facing mobility restrictions; this figure had surged to 21,000 by 22 August.
Since July 2024, the Colombian Government has been engaging in peace negotiations with the AGC. The group's sustained violent operations in southern Bolívar demonstrate either the fragility of these talks or the group's unwillingness to commit to agreed terms, risking negotiation collapse and prolonged conflict. The 2026 electoral cycle is also likely to heighten political violence across the country. NSAGs may intensify intimidation campaigns, restrict political expression, and coerce voters, creating an environment where electoral competition deteriorates into armed coercion. Civic leaders and community representatives are particularly exposed to the risks of co-option, threats, or silencing.
The escalation of armed confrontations and associated violence increases displacement, confinement, and the recruitment and exploitation of children by NSAGs.
Rural communities face compounding protection threats, including widespread landmine and improvised explosive device (IED) contamination impedes safe returns and perpetuates mobility restrictions, while small-scale miners and subsistence farmers – economically dependent on accessing disputed territories – face direct violence including threats, homicides, and forced displacement. This convergence of armed violence and environmental hazards creates a negative cycle where people are unable to work safely and communities cannot rebuild livelihoods, deepening both economic vulnerability. ([ICRC 27/03/2025](https://www.icrc.org/sites/default/files/media_file/2025-04/Humanitarian%20Report.pdf), [OCHA 22/08/2025](https://www.unocha.org/publications/report/mexico/latin-america-caribbean-weekly-situation-update-22-august-2025), [OCHA 08/08/2025](https://www.unocha.org/publications/report/haiti/latin-america-caribbean-weekly-situation-update-8-august-2025), [FIP 15/08/2025](https://ideaspaz.org/publicaciones/noticias/2025-08/asi-llega-el-clan-del-golfo-a-un-nuevo-intento-de-dialogos-de-paz-ahora-en-catar), [DP 24/08/2025](https://www.defensoria.gov.co/documents/20123/3322240/Resumen+AT+011-+2025.pdf/3647550f-af07-312b-b10d-c02392796b73?t=1756128768512), [DP 10/02/2025](https://www.defensoria.gov.co/-/defensor%C3%ADa-del-pueblo-alerta-sobre-crisis-humanitaria-en-el-sur-de-bol%C3%ADvar), [Humanitarian NGO Forum 30/09/2025](https://forohumanitariocolombia.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/Reclutamiento_foro_2025_eng.pdf), [OHCHR 25/06/2025](https://www.hchr.org.co/wp/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/07-10-2025-Information-note_ENG.pdf))

Trigger ID: R1013 - T0541
Title: Breackdown of peace talks
Description: 
Concerns are growing over the potential breakdown of peace negotiations between the Colombian Government and the Gaitanist Self-Defense Forces of Colombia (EGC), the largest and most influential non-state armed group in the country. According to official estimates, the EGC increased its membership by 95% between 2018 and 2024, reaching around 7,000 members—including 2,499 combatants and 4,563 support network members—by mid-2024. The group has expanded its territorial control in several departments, particularly Chocó, Magdalena Medio, southern Bolívar, and the Caribbean coast, where it has consolidated strategic corridors linked to illicit economies. Between 2023 and 2024, its armed capacity in southern Bolívar alone grew by 23%, highlighting a clear strengthening trend amid ongoing peace talks.
This continued military expansion and territorial consolidation raise doubts about the EGC’s genuine willingness to engage in disarmament or comply with potential peace accords. A collapse of the peace process could intensify clashes with other armed actors, notably the ELN and FARC-EP dissident factions, leading to further mass displacement, confinement, targeted killings, and restrictions on humanitarian access. The persistence of hostilities in areas such as southern Bolívar and the Magdalena Medio would likely deepen existing humanitarian crises, strain local institutional capacities, and expose civilian population, particularly rural communities, women, and children, to heightened protection risks.

Title: Increase in Electoral Violence 
Description: 
The 2026 electoral cycle in Colombia is taking place amid significant regional and national challenges. The assassination of Senator Miguel Uribe Turbay during a campaign rally in June 2025 marked the first killing of a presidential candidate in more than three decades, adding urgency to concerns about political violence. At the same time, the territorial presence and influence of NSAGs, restrict free political participation and undermine the integrity of electoral processes, particularly in conflict-affected regions like southern Bolívar.
The Early Electoral Warning (ATEL 2025–2026), issued by the Ombudsman’s Office, highlights the risks arising from the dominance, consolidation, coexistence, or territorial disputes of these armed groups. These dynamics may affect fundamental rights such as life, liberty, integrity, and security, as well as political and civil freedoms during the electoral period. In regions like southern Bolívar, where NSAGs exert de facto control, armed intimidation and fear limit the safe participation of both candidates and voters.
Among the risks identified by the  Ombudsman’s Office for areas such as southern Bolívar are manifestations of illegal armed governance, the capture of political representation, and mechanisms of population control by armed groups. These dynamics are compounded by the growing use of disinformation and manipulation through social media and artificial intelligence, which threaten the quality of public debate and weaken trust in institutions. As a result, social tension and localized electoral violence are likely to increase, particularly in territories where political competition intersects with criminal influence and coercion.

title: Failure of essential services owing to the blockade in Mali leads to civil unrest and destabilisation and aggravates needs
risk_type: Future impact of a hazard which has already taken place
rationale:
Since September 2025, Jama'a Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM), an Al Qaeda–affiliated group, has expanded its blockade strategy from the traditional conflict zones in northern and central Mali (Gao, Mopti, Tombouctou) to southern and southwestern regions, including Kayes, Koulikoro, and Ségou. This expansion signals a shift towards a strategy of coercive governance, with JNIM using economic strangulation – via targeted attacks on fuel convoys and the imposition of checkpoints along critical trade routes – to undermine state legitimacy and force power-sharing negotiations. The blockade marks the first large-scale attempt to encircle Bamako, Mali’s capital, and demonstrates the group’s increasing operational reach.
The blockades have resulted in acute shortages of fuel, electricity, and essential goods across the country. Fuel prices in Bamako surged by over 400% in October, with queues lasting hours and some car owners abandoning vehicles at petrol stations. Major public services, including health and education, have been severely disrupted. The Government closed schools and universities nationwide from 27 October to 9 November, citing the inability of staff and students to reach facilities amid the fuel crisis. Power cuts have intensified, and hospitals in peripheral cities, such as Sikasso and Koutiala, have reported severely limited operations. JNIM has enforced the blockade by destroying an estimated 200 fuel tankers since September, as well as killing at least 15 drivers and abducting others. The group has openly threatened transporters and companies attempting to defy the blockade. Humanitarian responders report that key corridors – particularly those linking Mali to Senegal and Côte d'Ivoire – are patrolled through armed checkpoints, and the Government is unable to maintain secure access despite military escorts. Several areas, such as Loulouni in the south and towns in Mopti and Gao, remain fully or partially isolated.
The humanitarian situation is likely to deteriorate further as a result of the blockade. Food insecurity, protection risks – particularly for women and girls – and displacement are expected to worsen amid prolonged service collapse. The blockades are likely to further destabilise Mali by directly undermining state authority and creating conditions for civil unrest. The fuel crisis caused by the blockade has led to the disruption of essential services, such as electricity, healthcare, water, and transportation, which are crucial for state legitimacy. When citizens cannot access hospitals, schools close, electricity fails for weeks, and food prices rise, they are likely to have a negative perception of the junta. The junta’s initial legitimacy came from promises of security and order; the blockades have destroyed both, leaving only the appearance of powerlessness. title: La Niña in Afghanistan worsens drought and leads to widespread agricultural losses, water scarcity, and acute food insecurity in 2026
rationale:
In Afghanistan, La Niña conditions started in October 2025 and are likely to persist until the February–March 2026 period. La Niña typically brings below-normal snowfall and rainfall combined with above-average temperatures in the country, driving drought-like conditions that significantly degrade agricultural productivity and water availability. Central, northeastern, northwestern, and western regions face a heightened risk of both agricultural and hydrological drought, directly threatening food security and rural livelihoods for farming and pastoralist communities. The current agricultural deficit reflects cumulative climate stress. In the 2024–2025 period, Afghanistan faced its fourth consecutive season of below-average production, with documented crop failures across eastern and northern areas. Dry conditions are likely to affect 2025 second-season crops (rice, cotton, and maize), most of which are harvested at the end of October, while forecasted below-average winter precipitation between November 2025 and January 2026 is likely to affect winter wheat production in 2026. Dry conditions also heighten concerns about fodder availability, likely affecting households dependent on pastoral income.
Below-average winter rainfall and snowfall are expected to curtail water availability in spring/summer, limiting irrigation, pasture growth, and snowmelt-fed rivers vital for agriculture and drinking water. Agricultural stress and water scarcity will compound the impact of recent seismic events. A series of earthquakes in 2025 destroyed homes and water/sanitation infrastructure while displacing tens of thousands, simultaneously triggering emergency shelter and WASH needs. Earthquake impacts, layered atop drought and flood shocks, have dramatically increased pressure on already-stretched community resources and humanitarian response. Population movements further intensify pressure on resources; over 2.6 million Afghans have returned from Iran and Pakistan since January 2025. These overlapping movements place severe strain on basic services, employment opportunities, and social cohesion in hosting communities, particularly in water-stressed border provinces. ([FEWS NET et al. 07/02/2025](https://reliefweb.int/attachments/07401c1b-0f71-46d4-810c-5e4e3a6064d1/2025_01_Afghanistan.pdf), [Mercy Corps 08/10/2025](https://www.mercycorps.org/press-room/releases/Crisis-Compounded-Afghanistan), [Alcis 01/07/2025](https://www.alcis.org/post/crop-estimates-for-six-provinces-in-afghanistan), [FEWS NET 06/10/2025](https://fews.net/middle-east-and-asia/afghanistan/key-message-update/september-2025), [FSC 02/2025](https://fscluster.org/sites/default/files/2025-02/Afghanistan%20EWIWG%20-%20Key%20messages%20Feb%202025.pdf))
hazard_materialisation: By March–April 2026, the climate-driven risk in Afghanistan has materialised into a worsening drought and food security crisis. Persistent La Niña conditions since late 2025 have resulted in below-average snowfall and rainfall and above-average temperatures, reducing water availability and damaging agricultural production. Additionally, spring water availability is significantly constrained because of weak snowpack and reduced snowmelt. ([Fews Net 04/2026](https://fews.net/middle-east-and-asia/afghanistan/seasonal-monitor/april-2026), [FAO 03/2026](https://openknowledge.fao.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/f46a1cd6-f0d8-4440-8829-2d0f4d051bfe/content))
impact_materialisation_description: The latest food insecurity projections indicate that over 17.4 million people are facing Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse food security levels between November 2025 and March 2026, reflecting declining crop yields and rural incomes. Spring water availability is significantly constrained because of weak snowpack and reduced snowmelt, limiting irrigation, pasture growth, and livestock productivity. Fodder shortages are increasingly affecting pastoral households. At the same time, the return of over 2 million Afghans from Iran and Pakistan continues to strain food systems and water resources, particularly in border provinces. ([FEWS Net 04/2026](https://fews.net/middle-east-and-asia/afghanistan/seasonal-monitor/april-2026), [FAO 06/04/2026](https://openknowledge.fao.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/f46a1cd6-f0d8-4440-8829-2d0f4d051bfe/content), [IPC 16/12/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/afghanistan/afghanistan-ipc-acute-food-insecurity-analysis-september-2025-september-2026-issued-16-december-2025))

Title: Below-average precipitation continuation
Description: 
The onset of a precipitation deficit serves as a key early-warning trigger in Afghanistan’s drought cycle, as sustained below-average rainfall reduces soil moisture, delays snow accumulation, and weakens river and groundwater recharge. According to the World Meteorological Organization and FEWS NET, such early deficits rapidly translate into water shortages that undermine winter crop growth and pasture regeneration, threatening food and income sources for farming and herding households. As water scarcity deepens, communities face heightened competition for limited resources, while reduced snowmelt later constrains drinking-water access. This chain reaction beginning with rainfall failure marks the start of humanitarian stress, often leading to displacement, rising food insecurity, and increased reliance on aid in the most drought-prone provinces

title: La Niña-driven above-normal rainfall and enhanced cyclonic activity in the Philippines cause widespread flooding, agricultural damage, and displacement
rationale: La Niña arrived in the Philippines in October 2025 and is likely to persist until February–March 2026. La Niña events have typically been linked to a higher frequency of tropical cyclones late in the year, along with increased rainfall and flood risk across much of the country. Current seasonal forecasts anticipate a high probability of above-average precipitation and above-average temperatures between November 2025 and March 2026. This indicates that between late 2025 and early 2026, the country could face compounding hazards, including storms and intense northeast monsoon rains, which may cause widespread flooding and landslides, especially across Luzon, Visayas, and Mindanao. Coastal and riverine communities in the Bicol region, Eastern Visayas, and Mindanao are particularly exposed, while informal urban settlements in Metro Manila and Cebu face a high risk of waterlogging and infrastructure collapse. Dam overflows and disrupted transport routes could isolate villages, delay aid delivery, and damage essential facilities, such as schools, health centres, and evacuation sites. The humanitarian consequences are expected to be severe: displacement, loss of livelihoods, and growing food insecurity among farming and fishing families. Waterborne and vector-borne diseases (such as leptospirosis, cholera, and dengue) may also surge because of stagnant floodwaters and poor sanitation. These risks will strain an already overburdened health system recovering from successive disasters. La Niña could push thousands of households into renewed crisis throughout the first half of 2026, amplifying humanitarian needs nationwide. ([PAGASA 26/08/2025](https://www.pagasa.dost.gov.ph/press-release/185), [NOAA 01/12/2025](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/analysis_monitoring/lanina/enso_evolution-status-fcsts-web.pdf), [PNA 26/08/2025](https://www.pna.gov.ph/articles/1257335))
hazard_materialisation: La Niña conditions, persisting through early 2026, enhanced cyclonic activity as anticipated. In November 2025, Typhoon Kalmaegi made multiple landfalls across the Visayas, affecting an estimated 2.4 million people, killing 153, and displacing over 377,000, with severe flooding, landslides, infrastructure damage, and WASH disruptions reported across eight regions. Super Typhoon Fung-Wong followed within days, affecting 2.7 million people and displacing 1.18 million. Combined agricultural losses from both storms exceeded PHP 4.14 billion, affecting over 84,000 farmers and tens of thousands of hectares of rice, high-value crops, and sugar cane. Tropical Storm Penha struck in February 2026, killing 12 and affecting over 700,000 people across Mindanao and the Visayas. Leptospirosis cases rose by 43% in the first half of 2025, with outbreaks consistently following flooding episodes.
impact_materialisation_description: Typhoon Tino made multiple landfalls across the Visayas between 2–6 November 2025. An estimated 2.4 million people across eight regions were affected, with over 377,000 displaced to either one of the 2,936 evacuation centres or staying with host families. 153 people died, 135 were injured, and 86 went missing, mostly in Western, Central, and Eastern Visayas. More than 12,600 homes were damaged or destroyed. Learning was disrupted for approximately 1.9 million students across five regions, with nearly 550 classrooms totally destroyed.

title: La Niña-induced heavy rainfall and enhanced cyclonic activity from October–March in central and northern Mozambique increase flooding and displacement
rationale: Forecasts indicate that weak La Niña conditions will persist through the October 2025 to March 2026 rainy season, typically bringing above-average rainfall to parts of southeastern Africa, including Mozambique. La Niña phases have historically coincided with heightened flood and cyclone risk, particularly along the Zambezi, Licungo, and Pungue River basins, as well as in low-lying coastal areas. The negative Indian Ocean Dipole further reinforces the likelihood of heavy and prolonged rainfall across the region. ([WMO 02/09/2025](https://wmo.int/media/news/la-nina-may-return-temperatures-are-likely-be-above-average), [WFP 15/10/2025](https://docs.wfp.org/api/documents/WFP-0000169538/download/), [FEWS NET 16/10/2025](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/international/FEWS_REPORT/Mozambique/FEWSNET_Mozambique_September2025.pdf))
hazard_materialisation: The La Niña‑induced hazard has fully materialised. Weak La Niña conditions persisted into the October 2025 to March 2026 rainy season, producing above‑average and prolonged rainfall across central and northern Mozambique. This resulted in repeated heavy rain events over already-saturated river basins, causing water in the Zambezi, Licungo, Pungoe, and Save Rivers to rise further and overflow. Cyclonic disturbances and low‑pressure systems in the Mozambique Channel intensified the hazard by generating short‑duration but high‑intensity rainfall, overwhelming drainage systems and weakening flood defences. The forecast hazard (excess rainfall, riverine flooding, and enhanced cyclone activity) transitioned into sustained hydrometeorological extremes, confirming full hazard materialisation.
impact_materialisation_description: The impacts have also materialised. Persistent flooding since December 2025 has triggered expanded inundation across Manica, Nampula, Sofala, Tete, and Zambezia, leading to continued evacuation (with at least 112,800 displaced), localised infrastructure damage, and crop losses. Saturated catchments and repeated flooding have disrupted community access, hindered service delivery, and contributed to worsening food insecurity by damaging or destroying agricultural fields. The strain on basic services has increased, particularly in low‑lying river basins and coastal districts, heightening risks of disease outbreaks by compromising water and sanitation systems. The situation has escalated from predicted impacts to tangible humanitarian consequences, confirming full impact materialisation.

title: La Niña-driven above-normal rainfall and tropical cyclone intensification cause widespread flooding, an increase in water-borne diseases and malnutrition
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale:
La Niña started in October 2025 and is expected to persist through February 2026. Historically, La Niña is associated with above-normal precipitation and increased tropical cyclone activity in Haiti, driving severe flooding, landslides, and water-borne disease outbreaks.
Seasonal forecasts indicate a very high probability of above-average precipitation between November 2025 and January 2026 and above-average temperatures until March 2026, across the whole country. While these anomalies will mostly occur outside the rainy season, which ends in November, flooding has become more common in recent years. La Nina-driven above-normal activity of the 2025 Atlantic hurricane season, which is expected to last until the end of November, may trigger additional flooding, landslides and damage—repeating destructive patterns seen from Tropical Storm Melissa in late October 2025. Crops' waterlogging in lower-lying agricultural zones may damage crops and reduce yields, to be harvested between December and March, compounding food supply shortages and driving food inflation. Rural populations already displaced by gang violence are particularly vulnerable to flooding, as damage to water and sanitation infrastructure may stretch already limited water, sanitation and hygiene conditions. In October 2025, there was a surge in cholera cases, especially in the West department. The combination of flooding and above-average temperatures may create favourable conditions for waterborne pathogens, increasing the risk of further spread of cholera and other waterborne diseases.
Additionally, flooding and landslides may damage or destroy homes, health infrastructure, and roads, forcing affected communities to relocate to other regions to seek refuge and humanitarian aid, increasing the number of people internally displaced. ([Fews Net 16/10/2025](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/international/FEWS_REPORT/Haiti/Current.pdf); [Copernicus Accessed 05/11/2025](https://climate.copernicus.eu/charts/packages/c3s_seasonal/products/c3s_seasonal_spatial_mm_rain_3m?area=area06&base_time=202510010000&type=tsum&valid_time=202512010000); [CPC 09/10/2025](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/analysis_monitoring/enso_advisory/ensodisc.shtml); [IPC 10/10/2025](https://www.ipcinfo.org/ipc-country-analysis/details-map/en/c/1159760/?iso3=HTI); [DTM Accessed 05/11/2025](https://dtm.iom.int/haiti))
hazard_materialisation: The risk has materialised as heavy rainfall between 29–30 April 2026 triggered flooding and rising river levels across the communes of Ouanaminthe and Ferrier in Haiti's Nord-Est department, affecting an estimated 15,000 people, with three injured and one missing. The floods killed livestock and damaged agricultural plains, over 3,660 houses, and several road networks. Departments such as Nord-Est have increasingly served as a refuge for IDPs escaping gang violence in departments such as Artibonite, Centre, and Ouest, meaning the impact of the floods may be compounding pre-existing needs. By December 2025, Nord-Est was hosting nearly 11,400 IDPs. The immediate needs of the flood-affected population include access to safe drinking water, WASH services, and waterborne disease prevention, alongside protection assistance for displaced people and other affected groups. ([OCHA 04/05/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/haiti/haiti-inondations-dans-le-departement-du-nord-est-flash-update-no-1-30-avril-2026?_gl=1*nq1hj9*_gcl_au*NDg0NTgzNTEuMTc3NjM2OTYxMg..*_ga*NDU4MTg0MzExLjE3Njg1NjMzNjI.*_ga_E60ZNX2F68*czE3Nzc5NDAyMTAkbzEwNyRnMSR0MTc3Nzk0MTIzMiRqMjgkbDAkaDA), [IOM 24/02/2026](https://dtm.iom.int/reports/haiti-report-internal-displacement-situation-round-12-december-2025?close=true))
impact_materialisation_description: The risk has materialised as heavy rainfall and flooding between 29–30 April 2026 affected an estimated 15,000 people, inundated more than 3,660 houses, damaged agricultural land, killed livestock, and disrupted road networks, restricting access to markets, basic services, and humanitarian assistance. The loss of crops and livestock is likely to reduce food availability and household income, particularly among vulnerable rural communities dependent on agriculture for their livelihoods. The floods also increased risks of displacement, shelter needs, and deteriorating living conditions, while standing water and damaged water infrastructure heightened the risk of waterborne diseases and increased needs for safe drinking water, sanitation, and hygiene support. Humanitarian needs include emergency shelter, food assistance, livelihood recovery, WASH services, and protection support. The impact is compounded by pre-existing displacement pressures, with Nord-Est hosting nearly 11,400 IDPs by December 2025 after receiving people fleeing violence elsewhere in Haiti. ([OCHA 04/05/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/haiti/haiti-inondations-dans-le-departement-du-nord-est-flash-update-no-1-30-avril-2026), [Sida 31/03/2026]( https://cdn.sida.se/app/uploads/2026/04/22144225/Haiti-HCA-2026_March-2026-Short.pdf), [OCHA 04/05/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/haiti/haiti-inondations-dans-le-departement-du-nord-est-flash-update-no-1-30-avril-2026))

title: La Niña-driven above-normal rainfall and flooding in Colombia cause widespread crop damage, landslides, waterborne diseases, and food insecurity and malnutrition
rationale:
An above-average rainy season is forecast for northern and northwestern Colombia through the remainder of 2025 and early 2026 (November–January), as La Niña conditions are expected to persist across the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean until the February–March 2026 period. This will likely lead to abundant rains, increasing the flood risk across Atlántico, northern Bolívar, Córdoba, La Guajira, Magdalena, Sucre, and the islands of San Andrés and Providencia department.
The second half of 2025 has already seen above-average rainfall, widespread flooding, and local and national response systems operating at full capacity, leaving the country more vulnerable to La Niña’s impacts. Heavy rainfall has affected almost 25,000 in just Bolívar, Córdoba, and Magdalena. Between November–January, rainfall is forecasted to increase by up to 30% in the regions expected to be affected, aggravating floods and landslides, damaging infrastructure, and destroying public buildings and main roads.
Flooding may affect crops and reduce agricultural production, particularly harming communities that rely on subsistence farming or that are already facing malnutrition. In 2025, 25% of households in Colombia faced consistent food access constraints, especially in rural communities, such as in Bolívar and La Guajira, which rely on their own crops for sustenance. Any disruption to the rice- and corn-growing cycles, which occur in November and December, would increase the limitations on these households' access to food.
The rains also limit the ability of affected communities to move freely in and out of their territories, effectively isolating them. Confinement decreases people’s ability to access essential services, such as health, education, and protection, meaning continued flooding would affect the livelihoods of these communities. This would worsen if the rains damage roads. Flooding will also worsen the humanitarian condition of the nearly 1.5 million people affected by violence-related incidents in Colombia from January–June 2025, marking the highest number in recent national history, particularly those displaced to the northern departments.
([CPC 13/11/2025](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/analysis_monitoring/enso_advisory/ensodisc_Sp.shtml), [CCO 26/09/2025](https://cco.gov.co/seguimiento-de-los-fenomenos-el-nino-la-nina-comunicado-no-09-de-2025/), [IDEAM 19/11/2025](https://bart.ideam.gov.co/wrfideam/new_modelo/CPT/informe/Informe.pdf), [IRI accessed 05/11/2025](https://iri.columbia.edu/our-expertise/climate/forecasts/seasonal-climate-forecasts/), [FEWS NET 27/11/2025](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/international/globalweatherhazard/Current.pdf), [El País 23/05/2025](https://elpais.com/america-colombia/2025-05-23/la-inseguridad-alimentaria-en-colombia-prevalece-en-las-areas-rurales-y-cae-en-las-zonas-urbanas.html), [OCHA accessed 24/11/2025](https://monitor.unocha.org/colombia))

title: Intensifying political violence approaching the February 2026 election in Bangladesh increases protection risks and constrains food, healthcare, and livelihood access
rationale:
Since the election announcement in December 2025, at least 16 political assassinations have been reported, predominantly targeting opposition figures. This reflects historical patterns in which contested electoral processes trigger targeted killings, intimidation, and cycles of retaliation. Primary perpetrators include supporters and affiliates of major political parties, including the Awami League, the Bangladesh Nationalist Party, Jamaat-e-Islami, and associated groups, as well as security forces enforcing restrictions on opposition activity. Weakening institutional control has also allowed opportunistic criminal groups to exploit the unrest and further contribute to lethal incidents. The continued circulation of weapons looted during the July 2024 uprising – numbering over 3,600, with many still unrecovered – compounds the security situation.
Repeated hartals and transport blockades, largely organised by opposition groups and met with security crackdowns, are deepening economic stress, particularly for urban poor populations reliant on daily wage labour and public transport. These disruptions are reducing household income, fuelling grievances, and heightening the risk of violent mobilisation in major urban centres such as Chattogram, Dhaka, and Rajshahi.
Within this volatile environment, religious minorities, particularly the Hindu community, face targeted attacks, including assaults on Hindu temples and cultural organisations, such as Bangladesh Udichi Shilpigoshthi, often following online hate campaigns. Taken together, these dynamics create conditions for a rapid escalation of political violence, with serious implications for civilian safety, livelihoods, and access to essential services. ([AJ 27/01/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/1/27/fear-and-hope-in-bangladesh-how-political-violence-is-haunting-elections), [The Financial Express 02/02/2026](https://thefinancialexpress.com.bd/national/political-violence-claims-158-lives-injures-thousands-in-17-months-tib), [AJ 01/02/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/2/1/deeply-insecure-why-bangladeshi-minorities-are-scared-ahead-of-elections), [BS 29/08/2025](https://www.business-standard.com/world-news/bangladesh-ec-calls-upcoming-election-most-risky-in-history-amid-unrest-125082901420_1.html), [Bangladesh Pratidin 07/11/2025](https://en.bd-pratidin.com/special/2025/11/07/50318), [Bangladesh Pratidin 31/08/2025](https://en.bd-pratidin.com/national/2025/08/31/45415), [TDS 14/10/2025](https://www.thedailystar.net/news/bangladesh/news/political-violence-hits-four-year-high-4010186))

title: A return to large‑scale conflict in Gaza stokes a further deterioration of food security and humanitarian conditions
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale:
On 10 October 2025, Hamas and Israel agreed upon a new ceasefire following two previous ones. The first lasted between 24–30 November 2023 and the second from 19 January to 18 March 2024, and both proved to be fragile. Under the 2025 agreement, Israel and Hamas committed to a withdrawal and unimpeded humanitarian access; Israel began marking a ‘yellow line’ on 20 October 2025 as a withdrawal boundary.
This new ceasefire is also likely to collapse owing to several factors: repeated violations, Israeli control of at least 60% of the strip, continued restrictions on humanitarian access, a recent UNSC decision that ignores Palestinians’ right to self-govern, and escalations related to the US/Israel attacks on Iran.
According to the Gaza Government Media Office, between 10 October and 22 December 2025, Israel committed at least 875 separate violations of the ceasefire, killing 114 Palestinians and wounding 1,112 others. Repeated Israeli violations may eventually prompt a response from Hamas, contributing to a collapse of the ceasefire and a return to full-blown conflict.
Under the ceasefire, Israel was supposed to withdraw to the yellow line, but reports show that Israeli military positions remain established across Gaza, controlling roughly 58–60% of the territory, including key areas in Rafah, Khan Younis, and parts of Gaza city. Israeli forces have also repeatedly crossed beyond this yellow line, occupying more areas than the ceasefire intended for the long term. This de facto occupation undermines the possibility of a stable ceasefire, and Palestinians are likely to perceive it as annexation.
Israeli forces continue to control the flow of humanitarian aid, goods, fuel, building materials, and humanitarian shelters into Gaza. Despite the ceasefire, many aid convoys and shipments remain blocked, and key supplies, such as tents, medical equipment, generators, and construction materials, have been rejected or delayed. Humanitarian needs in Gaza continue to be very high, especially during winter (typically from November–March). For example, Storm Byron resulted in widespread flooding in Gaza on 11 December, affecting 55,000 families. Without unimpeded access to aid, basic survival needs cannot be met, increasing hardships among the population and raising the incentive for armed groups to resume fighting.
On 17 November 2025, the UNSC adopted a resolution backing a US-proposed stabilisation plan for Gaza, including the deployment of an “international stabilisation force” and transitional governance structures. Many Palestinians reject the resolution, arguing that it disregards their right to self-determination and places Gaza under de facto foreign control. They view it as undermining legitimate Palestinian governance, making the renewal of armed resistance more likely if the stabilisation force appears as foreign occupation rather than protection.
If a war erupts between Israel and Iran, it will likely prompt Israel to close all border crossings into Gaza and potentially intensify air strikes. This will highly contribute to a return to conflict in Gaza and a collapse of the ceasefire.
A renewed war will likely begin with intense Israeli aerial bombardment across all areas west of the yellow line, targeting what Israel identifies as Hamas positions but inevitably hitting densely populated neighbourhoods where civilians are sheltering in damaged buildings or makeshift tents. Ground incursions may follow, especially in the central and southern areas, where Israeli forces already maintain forward positions. Urban fighting would expand again into Deir Al Balah, Khan Younis, and the remaining parts of Gaza city. It is also likely that Palestinian militias backed by Israel will be deployed to launch attacks on Hamas and loot humanitarian convoys. Inside Gaza, armed groups, mainly Hamas, would resume rocket fire and improvised attacks from the remaining pockets where they operate. This would prompt further Israeli strikes and expand the combat zone. ([ISPI 30/10/2025](https://www.ispionline.it/en/publication/gazas-limbo-fragile-ceasefire-and-the-roadblocks-to-trump-plans-phase-two-221961), [The Guardian 19/10/2025](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2025/oct/19/palestinians-in-gaza-fear-ceasefire-could-collapse-at-any-moment), [OHCHR 24/11/2025](https://www.ohchr.org/en/press-releases/2025/11/un-experts-urge-states-act-israeli-violations-threaten-fragile-gaza), [NPR 09/11/2025](https://www.npr.org/2025/11/09/nx-s1-5603399/the-fragile-truce-in-gaza-edges-toward-its-next-phase), [IBA 29/10/2025](https://www.ibanet.org/Israel-Gaza-A-Fragile-Ceasefire-leaves-region-wary), [AJ 22/12/2025](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2025/12/22/israel-kills-two-palestinians-in-gaza-city-as-ceasefire-violations-mount), [OCHA 18/12/2025](https://www.ochaopt.org/content/humanitarian-situation-update-349-gaza-strip))
hazard_materialisation: Although the October 2025 ceasefire was not formally terminated by July 2026, the hazard largely materialised, as hostilities intensified and humanitarian access deteriorated. Following the closure of Gaza's crossings on 1 March 2026, aid deliveries fell by around 80%, while Israel expanded military operations, controlling around 60% of the Gaza Strip by early June and announcing plans to seize 70% of the territory. Widespread evacuation orders and continued access restrictions further disrupted humanitarian operations.
impact_materialisation_description: The humanitarian impacts anticipated in the risk materialised. The sharp reduction in aid led to severe food shortages, with flour prices tripling and bread production declining by 50% because of shortages of flour and fuel. Humanitarian operations were disrupted, including World Central Kitchen reducing meal distributions by 50%. Malnutrition admissions increased by 21% between January–April compared with the same period in 2025, while food insecurity worsened as prolonged access restrictions and declining food availability further eroded households' already-depleted coping capacities.

rationale: The risk of violence following Uganda’s January 2026 general elections is driven by a documented pattern of militarised state response to political opposition and the erosion of civic space. title: Worsening energy shortages and U.S. pressure lead to essential service disruptions and rising humanitarian needs in Cuba
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale:
The reduction in Cuba’s oil imports – following the suspension of Venezuela’s daily supply of approximately 30,000 barrels and the continued pressure to prevent alternative sourcing from Mexico – has created an energy deficit equivalent to at least 30% of the country’s daily needs. Given Cuba’s reliance on imported fuel to operate even at reduced capacity, this shortfall is already contributing to prolonged power outages and fuel scarcity.
Over the next six months, unless alternative fuel supply arrangements materialise rapidly, the convergence of acute fuel supply disruption and structural economic fragility is likely to drive rapid and compounding humanitarian deterioration across Cuba. Power outages of 12–20 hours daily are already cascading across health, water, food, and social protection sectors in mutually reinforcing ways: hospitals losing electrical backup, ambulances unable to refuel, and refrigeration failures disrupting food imports collectively represent systemic stress – not isolated shocks – across interconnected service delivery chains. This trajectory is expected to further disrupt essential services, including water supply, healthcare, transportation, and food storage and distribution, while increasing economic pressure on households through rising prices and reduced availability of basic goods. At the same time, sustained energy and economic deterioration may intensify internal social strain and political instability, particularly amid active US efforts to incentivise political change, with potential consequences for civilian protection and humanitarian access. The geographic scope of disruption is countrywide, with disproportionate impacts in eastern provinces – including Santiago de Cuba and Holguin – and rural areas, where electricity availability has declined by up to 50% since January 2026.
Long-lasting power disruptions will compound the impact of extreme weather events, especially during the hurricane season (June–November). Cuba's aging grid and chronic blackouts make the country highly susceptible to hurricane damage, worsening fuel supply disruptions and extended outages. Fragile food production, reliant on cold chains and vulnerable crops, is routinely hit, with power failures spoiling perishables and storms destroying harvests, as exemplified by the impact of Hurricane Melissa in 2025.
As public services become increasingly unreliable, vulnerable populations – particularly older people, people with chronic illnesses, and low-income households – will likely face compounding protection and health risks. The progressive erosion of essential service delivery may in turn drive higher levels of internal displacement towards less-affected areas, as well as increased cross-border movement to countries with more stable economic conditions, further compounding regional humanitarian challenges.
([El Tiempo 20/01/2026](https://www.eltiempo.com/mundo/venezuela/sin-el-petroleo-de-venezuela-que-tan-cerca-esta-cuba-del-colapso-economico-total-analisis-de-mauricio-vargas-3525770); [EFE 18/01/2026](https://efe.com/economia/2026-01-18/cuba-bloqueo-petroleo-venezuela-efectos-crisis-energetica/); [EMOL 30/01/2026](https://www.emol.com/noticias/Internacional/2026/01/30/1190117/cuba-petroleo-energia-venezuela-mexico.html); [AJ 22/01/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/1/22/trump-seeking-regime-change-in-cuba-by-end-of-the-year-us-media-report))

title: The US–Iran escalation leads to strikes on Houthi-held ports, crippling infrastructure and disrupting vital humanitarian supply chains in Yemen
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale:
The de-facto authority (DFA) in the north of Yemen (also known as the Houthis) have pledged to respond to any US attack against Iran in early 2026, most likely by escalating Red Sea maritime attacks and launching direct strikes against Israel and US military bases in the region. By 19 February 2026, this risk had become imminent following a ten-day ultimatum issued by the US Administration for Iran to reach a nuclear and regional agreement, placing a potential military trigger in late February or early March. Any Houthi retaliatory attack would likely invite a renewed, intensified US or Israeli air campaign against Houthi military and economic infrastructure, with ports and other critical civilian infrastructure among the most likely targets.
Previous rounds of strikes have demonstrated the severe humanitarian consequences of this pattern. Israeli strikes on Sana’a between August–September 2025 killed at least 45 people and wounded over 230 others across multiple incidents, with residential areas, a fuel station supplying hospitals, and media offices among the sites struck. Al Hodeidah port – through which approximately 70% of Yemen's commercial imports and 80% of its humanitarian assistance pass – has been repeatedly targeted, with its operational capacity severely degraded. This infrastructure damage is compounded by access constraints stemming from the DFA's targeting of humanitarian organisations. The DFA has increasingly accused humanitarian responders of criminality, raided UN compounds, detained staff, and levelled accusations of espionage against aid workers. These raids and detentions have a cooling effect on NGOs working in DFA-controlled areas, with organisations reducing staffing to 'essential levels' and lowering operational risk thresholds, leading to reduced programming or withdrawal.
The WFP’s January 2026 decision to shut down operations and lay off all 365 staff in northern Yemen exemplifies this compounding effect, leaving 18 million people without humanitarian aid. This, alongside restrictions and the targeting of UN bodies and INGOs by the DFA, means the transfer of risks to grassroots organisations, which often serve as the first and sometimes only responders in remote areas.
A resumption of this pattern in the context of a wider US–Iran escalation would simultaneously degrade infrastructure and intensify humanitarian space contraction through the targeting of aid workers and facilities. With port damage reducing supply throughput and DFA harassment driving the withdrawal of major institutional responders, escalated strikes would compound humanitarian access constraints at a moment when Yemeni organisations – already bearing increased operational burden – face heightened political targeting. With 23.1 million people projected to be in need in 2026, this would deepen a severe humanitarian crisis.
([The Media Line 04/02/2026](https://themedialine.org/top-stories/can-protests-inside-iran-sever-the-houthis-umbilical-cord/), [Bloomberg 20/02/2026](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-02-20/trump-s-iran-ultimatum-sets-stage-for-strike-during-iaea-meeting), [AJ 10/09/2025](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2025/9/10/israel-attacks-yemen-capital-report), [TOI 24/08/2025](https://www.timesofisrael.com/iaf-strikes-yemens-capital-after-houthis-fired-cluster-bomb-missile-over-weekend/), [UN 14/07/2025](https://news.un.org/en/story/2025/07/1165395), [SCR 12/07/2025](https://www.securitycouncilreport.org/whatsinblue/2025/07/yemen-votes-on-draft-resolutions-extending-unmhas-mandate-and-the-houthi-red-sea-attacks-reporting-requirement.php), [UNSC 12/09/2025](https://www.securitycouncilreport.org/whatsinblue/2025/07/yemen-votes-on-draft-resolutions-extending-unmhas-mandate-and-the-houthi-red-sea-attacks-reporting-requirement.php))

title: Potential Red Sea disruptions from a US–Iran conflict reduce foreign currency earnings, heighten food insecurity, and disrupt services across Egypt
rationale: Red Sea disruptions linked to attacks by the de-facto authority (DFA) in the north of Yemen (also known as the Houthis) since October 2023 have left an economic impact on Egypt, and an escalation involving the US and Israel against Iran is likely to have a similar impact. This is because Egypt’s economy is highly dependent on Suez Canal transit fees for foreign currency earnings. Another Red Sea de facto blockade may lead to a sharp decline in Suez Canal traffic by up to 40% similar to the drop reported between December 2023 and January 2024, potentially reducing its revenues by 50%. Those revenues often generate around 2.2% of Egypt’s GDP and up to one-quarter of its foreign currency earnings. Reduced foreign currency would increase the cost of key imports, including wheat and cooking oil. During the 12-Day War in June 2025, Israel halted gas supplies to Egypt, which cover 15–20% of its domestic consumption. Renewed disruptions to Israeli gas supplies, which account for 15% of Egypt’s electricity generation and are foundational to Egyptian fertiliser producers, could lead to prolonged power cuts, market disruptions, and agricultural impacts. ([UNCTAD 26/01/2024](https://unctad.org/news/red-sea-black-sea-and-panama-canal-unctad-raises-alarm-global-trade-disruptions), [ICG 16/05/2024](https://reliefweb.int/report/egypt/crisis-group-middle-east-and-north-africa-briefing-ndeg91-egypts-gaza-dilemmas-enar), [fDi Intelligence 13/06/2025](https://www.fdiintelligence.com/content/0777017b-6d58-48e1-8357-e80a28822d08), [IMF 31/01/2024](https://www.imf.org/en/Publications/REO/MECA/Issues/2024/01/31/regional-economic-outlook-update-mena-january-2024), [ACAPS 10/02/2026](https://indd.adobe.com/view/8a01ba30-9b69-4956-b211-b036d59689c5))
impact_materialisation_description: The anticipated impacts partially materialised through wider conflict-related disruptions, with food inflation reaching an estimated 28% by March 2026, fertiliser prices rising by 75–87% by May, the Egyptian pound depreciating by 14% in the first month of the conflict, and power cuts exceeding two hours daily persisting in parts of Cairo and Giza through the March–April period. The anticipated Red Sea disruption did not materialise. Although DFA attacks and threats against shipping increased in July, prompting some vessels to reroute or reverse course, there was no sustained blockade of the Bab Al Mandab Strait or major disruption to Suez Canal traffic and operations. Canal revenue rose by 13% in the second quarter of 2026, though this reflects tanker traffic rerouted via the Suez corridor owing to the Strait of Hormuz closure rather than a genuine security-driven recovery in Red Sea shipping. ([Middle East Insider 04/04/2026](https://themiddleeastinsider.com/2026/04/04/iran-war-impact-egypt-economy-5-numbers-2026/), [The New Arab 15/05/2026](https://www.newarab.com/news/egypts-farmers-hit-iran-war-price-surge), [TIMEP 04/06/2026](https://timep.org/2026/06/04/a-balancing-act-in-a-rentier-reality-egypt-and-the-iran-war/), [Reuters 30/07/2026](https://www.reuters.com/business/energy/drone-strike-egypt-sparks-security-concerns-about-suez-oil-exports-2026-07-30/), [Reuters 31/07/2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/imf-completes-egypt-reviews-unlocks-18-billion-2026-07-31/), [CBE 09/07/2026](https://www.cbe.org.eg/en/news-publications/news/2026/07/09/17/02/mpc-press-release-9-july-2026), [The Rio Times 14/08/2026](https://www.riotimesonline.com/suez-canal-revenue-second-quarter-2026))

title: Hezbollah–Israel escalation related to Israeli/United States attack on Iran results in increased internal displacement, cross-border movements, and worsening food insecurity
rationale: A renewed escalation of clashes between Hezbollah and Israel is likely to happen in parallel with US and Israeli attacks on Iran. Hezbollah is perceived as a proxy of Iran and has already stated that it will not remain neutral if Iran is attacked, and Israel considers Hezbollah a major threat to its national security. The conflict dynamics in a future escalation may be largely similar to the September–November 2024 escalation, with some key differences. First, Hezbollah has been significantly weakened following the assassination of several senior leaders, disrupted arms and funding routes from Iran through Syria after the fall of Al Assad on 8 December 2024, and reduced service provision capacity within Hezbollah’s area of influence, increasing civilian reliance on humanitarian assistance. Second, the Lebanese Government, under international pressure, continues to attempt to disarm Hezbollah, increasing the likelihood of an internal conflict. Third, displacement dynamics will likely differ from previous escalations. Displaced Lebanese people may not consider crossing to Syria, since they perceive the new Syrian Government to have a hostile stance towards Hezbollah, likely increasing internal displacement. Syrian refugees may return to Syria if insecurity increases in Lebanon, however. Between September–December 2024, over 562,000 people crossed into Syria from Lebanon, with 63% being Syrians and 37% Lebanese, all of whom required urgent protection, shelter, food, WASH, and health services. ([Geopolitical Monitor 07/11/2025](https://www.geopoliticalmonitor.com/israeli-hezbollah-strikes-toward-a-new-conflict/), [FDD 27/01/2026](https://www.fdd.org/analysis/2026/01/27/hezbollah-we-will-not-remain-neutral-if-islamic-republic-endangered/), [TV7 27/01/2026](https://www.tv7israelnews.com/vod/series/18738/?episode-id=RTr7v66vvD4), [MENAF 02/06/2025](https://manaramagazine.org/2025/06/hezbollah-in-decline-between-resistance-rhetoric-and-strategic-reality/), [Atlantic Council 15/04/2025](https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/blogs/menasource/weakened-by-israel-hezbollah-turns-to-spin-games-to-hold-support/), [The Conversation 08/12/2025](https://theconversation.com/with-a-deadline-looming-lebanon-is-under-pressure-to-disarm-hezbollah-or-risk-another-war-271523), [UNHCR 06/02/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/lebanon/lebanon-glance-escalation-hostilities-lebanon-06-february-2025-enar))

title: A contested April 2026 electoral process in Libya heightens localised armed clashes, displacement, and service disruptions
rationale:
Amid a stalled UN-backed political process and deep institutional fragmentation, political tensions in Libya will likely increase over the next three to six months around the April 2026 presidential and parliamentary elections and ensuing impacts.
The immediate political context is marked by institutional paralysis. Disputes between the east-based House of Representatives (HoR) and the Tripoli-based High Council of State (HCS) over the reconstitution of the High National Election Commission (HNEC) board have stalled the electoral timeline. On 29 December 2025, the HoR voted to fill vacant HNEC board seats, prompting the HCS head to accuse the HoR speaker of violating the UN-backed political agreement. On 5 January 2026, the HCS elected a new HNEC president, triggering objections from eastern authorities. UNSMIL publicly warned on 6 January that these escalatory steps risk undermining the political process. By mid-February, UNSMIL reported “no meaningful progress” on agreeing to election rules or forming a unified Government.
Several triggers could spark election-related violence. First, unilateral actions by either side on electoral institutions or rules risk provoking armed responses from rival authorities and affiliated militias. Second, the proposed UNSMIL structured dialogue risks reinforcing existing power imbalances, particularly if perceived as bypassing key stakeholders or legitimising contested authorities. Third, rising economic pressure – including fuel shortages, declining living standards, and the devaluation of the Libyan dinar by nearly 15% on 18 January – is deepening public frustration. Fourth, escalating security incidents and assassinations are heightening tensions. Most notably, the killing of Saif al-Islam Gaddafi on 3 February, followed by a prosecutor-led investigation announced on 5 February without visible accountability measures, may reinforce perceptions that armed groups can carry out political violence with impunity, contributing to heightened tensions and fears of politically motivated targeting.
If violence erupts, it will most likely take the form of localised armed clashes between rival armed groups aligned with eastern and western authorities instead of conflict on nationwide front lines. High-risk areas include Tripoli and its surroundings, where competing militias operate; Benghazi city and eastern Libya, where tensions between political authorities and security forces persist; and southern border areas, where armed groups and criminal networks are active. Violence could include targeted killings, attacks on electoral institutions, the intimidation of political figures, and clashes over strategic infrastructure. Given Libya’s history, even limited clashes could trigger localised displacement, disrupt basic services, and restrict humanitarian access, particularly in urban centres and contested southern regions.
Regional involvement, including Tunisia’s February proposal with Algeria and Egypt in coordination with UNSMIL, may help reduce tensions by supporting a Libyan-led dialogue. Without agreement among Libyan authorities and armed groups, however, it is unlikely to prevent election-related violence. ([TNA 03/11/2025](https://www.newarab.com/analysis/libyas-18-month-gamble-uns-political-roadmap-nowhere), [TNA 05/02/2026](https://www.newarab.com/news/libya-probes-killing-late-ruler-gaddafis-son), [AJ 27/01/2026](https://www.aljazeera.net/news/2026/1/27/%D8%AA%D9%88%D9%86%D8%B3-%D8%AA%D9%82%D8%AA%D8%B1%D8%AD-%D8%AA%D9%86%D8%B8%D9%8A%D9%85-%D9%85%D8%A4%D8%AA%D9%85%D8%B1-%D8%AC%D8%A7%D9%85%D8%B9-%D9%84%D8%AD%D9%84-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A3%D8%B2%D9%85%D8%A9), [ICG accessed 24/02/2026](https://www.crisisgroup.org/crisiswatch/january-trends-and-february-alerts-2026), [Peace News 16/02/2026](https://peacenews.com/fragmentation-governance-and-the-limits-of-political-settlement-and-peacebuilding-in-libya/), [UNSC 18/02/2026](https://press.un.org/en/2026/sc16298.doc.htm))

title: The US/Israel–Iran escalation affecting the Strait of Hormuz drives conflict, food insecurity, livelihood collapse, and protection risks in Iraq
rationale:
A US–Iran confrontation triggered by a ten-day ultimatum issued by the US administration for Iran to reach a nuclear and regional agreement (placing a potential military trigger in late February or early March 2026) could increase humanitarian needs in Iraq through two compounding mechanisms: direct Iranian proxy escalation via the Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) and broader regional economic disruption, including potential closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
Following the fall of Bashar Al Assad's regime in Syria and Israel's weakening of Hezbollah in Lebanon and Syria, Iraq has become a significant regional asset for Iran. The PMF, an official Iraqi security institution composed largely of Iran-backed militias, represents Iran's likely vector for retaliation against US interests in Iraq. Kata'ib Hezbollah, the largest militia within the PMF, has publicly warned of military response if Iran is attacked.
Iraq's political trajectory compounds this risk. Government formation remains contested between the US administration and Iraq's Coordination Framework over the composition of leadership, with the Trump administration threatening to cut Iraq off from its oil revenues if a candidate closely aligned with Iran and the PMF assumes the premiership. Sitting Prime Minister Al Sudani actively restrained the PMF during the June 2025 Iran–Israel conflict, but a pro-Iran administration would significantly increase militia escalation risk. Political instability, combined with PMF escalation, would likely worsen conditions for Iraq's approximately one million IDPs and deepen sectarian tensions.
Beyond direct proxy conflict, a US–Iran confrontation could trigger humanitarian needs through economic disruption. Prior to the escalation, over 90% of Iraq's oil was exported through the Strait of Hormuz, with the remaining oil exported through the currently closed Ceyhan pipeline connected to Türkiye via Iraq's autonomous Kurdish region. A potential closure of the strait would eliminate Iraq's primary export route, driving oil price shocks that cascade through Iraq's oil-dependent economy and creating pressure on government services and humanitarian response capacity at a moment when political instability already constrains governance. title: Direct US–Iran military confrontation causes mass civilian casualties in Iran and regional conflict spillover, leading to displacement and service collapse
rationale:
Since January 2026, US–Iran tensions have intensified significantly, with the US assembling the largest military force in the region since the 2003 Iraq invasion. Iranian officials’ rhetoric and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz for military drills on 17 February 2026 demonstrate Iran's willingness to escalate if attacked.
The most probable escalation pathway begins with limited US air strikes targeting strategic Iranian sites, prompting Iranian retaliation through ballistic missile attacks against US military bases in the region, proxy attacks on regional responders, or the closure or militarisation of the Strait of Hormuz. This would trigger US counter-retaliation against Iranian military assets and command structures, potentially expanding the conflict through an escalatory spiral involving Iranian proxies in Yemen, Gulf states facing missile and drone threats, and Israel conducting strikes on Iranian targets, ultimately transforming bilateral US–Iran confrontation into a protracted regional war with multi-front humanitarian consequences.
Direct US military strikes against Iranian strategic targets will likely trigger immediate humanitarian deterioration through mass civilian casualties, critical infrastructure damage, acute protection crises, displacement, and the collapse of already-strained essential services, affecting millions of Iranians and Afghan refugees. ([Reuters 23/02/2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/us-pulling-non-essential-staff-embassy-beirut-amid-iran-tensions-2026-02-23/), [AJ 24/02/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/2/24/trump-hits-out-at-reports-that-top-general-flagged-risks-of-attacking-iran), [TWP 23/02/2026](https://www.washingtonpost.com/national-security/2026/02/23/dan-caine-iran-risk-trump/), [AJ 24/02/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/2/24/iran-cannot-defeat-us-military-might-but-it-can-still-win))
hazard_materialisation:
Direct US–Israel attack materialised in Iran as a large-scale, coordinated military operation rather than a limited strike. On 28 February 2026, the United States and Israel launched a pre-emptive offensive targeting Iran’s nuclear facilities, missile systems, and military infrastructure. The attack began with an intensive first wave of hundreds of air and missile strikes within hours, reflecting a high-intensity “shock and awe” strategy.
A key feature was the targeting of senior leadership and command structures, aimed at disrupting decision-making and weakening state capacity. The operation also involved multi-domain warfare, combining precision airstrikes with intelligence-driven targeting and cyber capabilities.
Strikes were conducted simultaneously across multiple locations, including Tehran and other strategic sites, indicating a nationwide campaign rather than isolated attacks. Overall, the hazard materialised as a systematic, high-intensity military campaign designed to rapidly degrade Iran’s strategic capabilities.
impact_materialisation_description:
The anticipated escalation scenario has largely materialised in Iran following the outbreak of hostilities on 28 February 2026. Initial US–Israeli airstrikes on strategic military and nuclear sites quickly triggered Iranian retaliation through missile and drone attacks, leading to a sustained, multi-day conflict not only in Iran, rather to the region particularly in the gulf countries. In Iran, strikes expanded beyond military targets into across the country, causing over 1,937 civilian deaths and more than 24,800 injuries by March 2026, alongside damage to hospitals, schools, and civilian buildings.
The conflict has caused severe disruption to essential services. Damage to healthcare facilities has overwhelmed hospitals, while attacks on water and industrial infrastructure have reduced access to safe water, electricity, and fuel, and increased environmental health risks.
Mass displacement has begun, with over 3.2 million people internally displaced in Iran by 12 March 2026, and numbers expected to rise. Vulnerable groups, including Afghan refugees, face heightened protection risks and reduced access to services.
The conflict has also regionalised, with threats to maritime security around the Strait of Hormuz, reinforcing the risk of a prolonged, multi-front humanitarian crisis affecting millions.

title: The escalation of political and armed conflict in Southwest state leads to large‑scale displacement and worsens humanitarian conditions
rationale:
Rising tensions between Southwest state authorities and the Federal Government of Somalia continue to significantly increase the probability of armed confrontation and large‑scale displacement in the coming weeks and months. The formal severing of ties with Mogadishu, federal declarations that the Southwest leadership’s mandate has expired, and mutual accusations over the diversion of weapons and security interference point to a deepening political rift. Around Baidoa, deployment orders for regional forces and reported movements of federal troops indicate an elevated risk of localised clashes escalating into a wider confrontation, particularly if no negotiated settlement is reached before key political milestones. Upcoming electoral processes in Southwest state and nationwide are likely to further heighten tensions, as competition over power and representation may trigger protests, the contestation of results, or targeted violence around Baidoa and other strategic locations.
At the same time, Southwest state faces severe and compounding humanitarian pressures that would heighten the impact of any political or security escalation. Prolonged drought has already driven mass internal displacement from districts such as Waajid and other parts of Bay and Bakool, eroding pastoral and agropastoral livelihoods and sharply increasing food insecurity. Many displaced families have moved towards Baidoa and other already-overstretched host areas, where services, water availability, and livelihood opportunities are extremely limited. Further conflict‑related displacement from urban centres or along key road corridors would add to existing caseloads, strain coping capacity, and heighten protection risks, including family separation, exploitation, and gender‑based violence. In a context of recurrent access constraints and insecurity, even a temporary disruption of humanitarian operations around Baidoa or in drought‑affected rural areas could quickly translate into sharp deteriorations in food security, health, and protection conditions for hundreds of thousands of people. Overall, the combination of unresolved federal–state tensions, upcoming electoral contests, and severe climatic stress maintains a high probability that political and armed escalation in Southwest state could trigger large‑scale displacement and a rapid deterioration of humanitarian conditions, even though a full‑scale armed confrontation has not yet occurred.
([Mustaqbal Media 22/03/2026](https://mustaqbalmedia.net/en/somalia-announces-start-of-nationwide-elections-amid-political-tensions/?utm_source=feedly&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=somalia-announces-start-of-nationwide-elections-amid-political-tensions), [SG 21/03/2026](https://www.somaliguardian.com/news/somalia-news/southwest-somalia-president-orders-regional-forces-to-counter-federal-troops/), [Reuters 17/03/2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/somalias-south-west-state-says-it-has-severed-ties-with-federal-government-2026-03-17/), [Hiiraan 23/03/2026](https://www.hiiraan.com/security4/2026/Mar/204725/southwest_parliament_speaker_accuses_federal_government_of_diverting_egyptiansupplied_weapons.aspx), [Mustaqbal Media 22/03/2026](https://mustaqbalmedia.net/en/federal-government-declares-end-of-south-west-leadership-term-amid-deepening-political-tensions/))

Southwest State President Laftagareen resigned and fled to Kenya. Further clashes between federal forces and Laftagareen loyalists erupted on the outskirts of Baidoa in late May 2026. Elections in Southwest State are currently underway amid continued instability. ([UNHCR 01/04/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/somalia/flash-12-over-50000-people-displaced-following-political-escalation-baidoa-south-west-state), [Garowe Online 22/05/2026](https://www.garoweonline.com/en/news/somalia/somalia-clashes-erupt-outside-baidoa-between-federal-troops-and-forces-loyal-to-ousted-southwest-leader), [Hiiraan 27/05/2026](https://www.hiiraan.com/security4/2026/May/205279/heavy_fighting_erupts_near_baidoa_between_federal_forces_and_laftagareen_loyalists.aspx))

Displaced populations faced heightened protection risks including overcrowding, inadequate shelter, and gender-based violence exposure, compounding already severe drought-related displacement and food insecurity across Bay and Bakool. Some families have begun returning, though conditions remain fragile. Broader risks related to the federal–state constitutional tensions are captured under the Somalia constitutional crisis risk. title: Intercommunal tensions between IDPs and host communities in Lebanon result in localised clashes and further displacement
rationale:
Rising intercommunal tensions between host communities and IDPs in Lebanon have intensified by late March 2026 amid large-scale displacement and mounting socioeconomic pressure. The re-escalation of hostilities between Hezbollah and Israel since 1 March has displaced an estimated 1.2 million people, mostly from southern Lebanon.
Reports indicate growing host community fatigue, with increasing complaints over overcrowding, pressure on basic services, and the repurposing of schools and public buildings into collective shelters, disrupting education and raising concerns over some IDP sites becoming permanent sites rather than temporary ones.
Besides the high number of IDPs, many other factors drive the tensions, including economic deterioration, rising fuel and commodity prices, and a highly polarised information environment that is fuelling sectarian tensions between Shia and Christian/Sunni populations. Misinformation, especially on social media, including security-related rumours and anti-IDP rhetoric are fuelling tensions. Host communities also express security concerns, fearing that the presence of IDPs may expose their areas to Israeli air strikes. Already, OCHA has reported instances of intercommunal tensions within host communities, although their nature is unclear.
Further escalation may emerge from additional waves of displacement, the expansion of Israeli military operations in southern Lebanon, and Israeli air strikes on areas considered ‘safe’ for IDPs. For example, between 12–13 March 2026, Israeli air strikes expanded into residential areas hosting IDPs in Beirut and Mount Lebanon, killing at least eight people and injuring several others. Such attacks on what is perceived as ‘safe areas’ are heightening tensions between host communities and IDPs.
These dynamics are likely to translate into localised clashes over the next three to six months as displacement continues, particularly in high-density urban areas where resources are scarce and governance is weak. Clashes are most likely between host community residents and IDPs (the majority of whom are Shia) but may also involve civic authorities or security forces enforcing restrictive measures. Such clashes are likely to increase insecurity and fatalities and drive further displacement, particularly for already displaced populations. The risk is assessed as Medium, as key triggers, including large-scale displacement, host community pressure, and rising anti-IDP rhetoric are already present, and recent incidents indicate increasing tensions; however, while widespread intercommunal violence is unlikely, the probability of localised incidents remains significant. ([UNDP 30/03/2026](https://admin.tms-lebanon.com/StaticFiles/Files/TMS_Tensions_Pulse_-_30_March_2026.pdf), [UNHCR 30/03/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/lebanon/middle-east-situation-lebanon-flash-update-4-23-29-march-2026), [Megaphone 30/03/2026](https://megaphone.news/oped/%D9%87%D9%84-%D9%85%D8%A7-%D8%B2%D8%A7%D9%84-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A8%D9%84%D8%AF-%D9%85%D9%85%D9%83%D9%86%D8%A7), [OCHA 21/03/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/lebanon/lebanon-flash-update-10-escalation-hostilities-lebanon-19-march-2026), [IM Lebanon 13/03/2026](https://www.imlebanon.org/2026/03/13/lebanon-1389/))

title: Escalating violence between the Sudan People's Liberation Movement and the Sudan People's Liberation Movement-in-Opposition reignites civil war, driving mass displacement and service collapse
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale:
The collapse of the 2018 revitalized peace agreement and the disbandment of the unity government have dramatically increased the risk of South Sudan sliding back into full-scale civil conflict. The March 2025 arrest of First Vice President Riek Machar of the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-in-Opposition by President Salva Kiir has reignited ethnically charged fighting between Dinka and Nuer armed forces, with clashes already concentrated in Jonglei and Upper Nile states. Up to 300,000 newly displaced people add to the approximately two million already internally displaced and over ten million – two-thirds of the population – requiring some form of humanitarian assistance, including 7.5 million projected to face food insecurity during the April–July lean season. South Sudan has suffered from chronic violence since independence. The collapse of the peace framework ahead of elections, accompanied by the re-emergence of organised, ethnically mobilised armed groups, represents the risk of a return to full-scale civil war.
Several factors increase the likelihood of deterioration into civil war. The taking and retaking of Akobo signals an escalation beyond the fragmented, subnational violence that characterised the 2018–2024 period, with organised armed groups now contesting territory at a scale not seen since the first civil war. The mobilisation of Nuer armed groups, including the White Army, suggests this is a coordinated insurgency with the capacity to sustain prolonged fighting. Uganda's continued deployment of troops in support of Kiir's Government risks drawing the conflict into a broader regional confrontation, and spillover from Sudan and Ethiopia could further destabilise border areas. Over 1.36 million people have already arrived in South Sudan from Sudan since April 2023, with services in border areas stretched to breaking point; an additional 380,000 arrivals are projected by the end of 2026. The planned December 2026 elections, already twice postponed, will intensify political competition and may become a flashpoint for renewed violence, whether they proceed or are cancelled again. ([ICG 25/03/2026](https://www.crisisgroup.org/cmt/africa/south-sudan/halting-south-sudans-slide-war), [ISS 30/03/2026](https://issafrica.org/iss-today/race-against-time-to-stabilise-south-sudan-as-elections-loom), [OCHA 12/02/2026](https://www.unocha.org/publications/report/south-sudan/south-sudan-humanitarian-needs-and-response-plan-2026-january-2026), [OCHA 16/04/2026](https://www.unocha.org/publications/report/south-sudan/south-sudan-humanitarian-update-1-17-april-2026), [MSF 30/01/2026](https://www.msf.org/south-sudan-government-blocks-opposition-held-areas-humanitarian-access))
