title: Prolonged fuel shortages in Bangladesh worsen food security and disrupt health, telecommunications, and other essential services
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale:
Geopolitical shocks, import dependency, and market distortions risk a prolonged or widespread fuel shortage across Bangladesh, worsening the humanitarian situation. The country imports about 95% of its petroleum – 63% from Iraq, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates via the Strait of Hormuz. The 2026 war between Israel–US and Iran has disrupted this corridor, constraining imports; continued disruptions would further limit fuel supply. Despite diversifying imports towards the US after a February 2026 trade deal, alternative routes are unable to replace Middle Eastern volumes at scale, leaving near-term shortfall risks.
Bangladesh's capacity to absorb disruptions is eroding as economic conditions worsen. Inflation reached 9.13% in February 2026, and Bangladesh Petroleum Corporation import costs rose by 29% year-on-year. Pressure on foreign exchange reserves, including reduced remittance inflows from the Gulf countries affected by the war, may constrain fuel imports. Distribution practices – hoarding, panic-buying, and first-come-first-served allocation – further limit access.
These supply constraints are converging with peak seasonal demand during Boro season – the December–May dry-season rice cultivation period that accounts for around 55% of annual production. Should fuel shortages persist through this period, the consequences for food security are likely to be severe. Limited diesel availability and government policies such as a two-litre-per-visit rationing cap are constraining irrigation, especially in northern districts, where demand exceeds supply. Farmers report shortages of both diesel and electricity. If constraints persist, rice output will likely fall and, with higher fuel-driven transport costs, raise staple food prices, disproportionately affecting low-income households already spending most of their earnings on food.
Given continued Hormuz disruptions, Bangladesh's import dependency, and deteriorating economic conditions, fuel shortages are likely to persist or worsen over the next three to six months, with cascading consequences for food security and essential services. ([ORF 16/04/2026](https://www.orfonline.org/expert-speak/beyond-diversification-bangladesh-s-fuel-crisis-and-role-of-neighbourhood-ties), [AJ 09/03/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/3/9/bangladesh-shuts-universities-limits-fuel-sale-as-iran-war-causes-shortage), [DT 29/03/2026](https://www.dhakatribune.com/bangladesh/406405/diesel-crisis-disrupts-irrigation-in-northern), [TDS 10/03/2026](https://www.thedailystar.net/news/bangladesh/news/diesel-crunch-hits-farm-heartlands-4125026), [TDS 31/03/2026](https://www.thedailystar.net/opinion/news/how-bangladesh-can-manage-fuel-shocks-economic-stability-4139506), [Prothom Alo 21/04/2026](https://en.prothomalo.com/amp/story/bangladesh/local-news/ai8kcp4avr), [TDS 07/04/2026](https://www.thedailystar.net/opinion/news/how-hoarding-and-panic-buying-are-deepening-the-fuel-crisis-4145366), [TBS 13/04/2026](https://www.tbsnews.net/bangladesh/energy/fuel-imports-14-costs-jump-29-so-why-shortage-1410106))
hazard_materialisation: The hazard materialised in August 2026 as persistent gas and liquefied natural gas (LNG) shortages translated into severe power supply disruptions and reduced industrial activity. On 3 August, average power generation shortfalls reached 1,482MW, with shortages reported across 62 of 143 generating units. Shortages were particularly acute in Dhaka, Khulna, Mymensingh, Rajshahi, and Rangpur divisions. By 18 August, power plants were receiving only 37.4% of their gas requirement, leaving 13 of 25 affected units unable to generate electricity. On 19 August, the Excelerate LNG terminal at Moheshkhali, Cox’s Bazar, ran out of LNG, reducing national gas supply to 2,185mmcfd against demand of around 3,800mmcfd. ([The Daily Star 03/08/2026](https://www.thedailystar.net/news/bangladesh/news/gas-shortage-sparks-extensive-power-cuts-4238811), [BD News24 18/08/2026](https://bdnews24.com/bangladesh/3746b783d5b0), [The Business Standard 19/08/2026](https://www.tbsnews.net/bangladesh/energy/excelerate-fsru-halts-supply-again-four-days-after-resumption-1519786))
impact_materialisation_description: During August, gas and electricity shortages disrupted industrial production, transport, and household electricity access in Bangladesh. A temporary improvement in LNG supplies reduced load-shedding, but gas shortages continued to constrain industrial activity. Higher operating and transport costs, poultry losses, and rising food prices further reduced household purchasing power, while factory closures threatened workers’ incomes. Agricultural production also came under increasing pressure. Despite adequate national fertiliser stocks, localised shortages, distribution constraints, and prices above official rates limited farmers’ access to inputs and could affect upcoming harvests. An estimated five million people are in need of agricultural assistance between June–November 2026, indicating a further deterioration in livelihoods and food availability. title: El Niño-driven above-average temperatures and below-average precipitation cause widespread drought in the Central American Dry Corridor (El Salvador, Guatemala, and Honduras), increasing food and health needs
risk_type: Future impact of a hazard which has already taken place
rationale: El Niño is very likely to emerge by July 2026 and persist until December 2026 to February 2027. Between June–August 2026, seasonal forecasts anticipate a high probability of above-average temperatures and below-average precipitation associated with El Niño across the Central American Dry Corridor, an arid region that spans from eastern Guatemala, northern El Salvador, and southern and southwestern Honduras. The region is highly vulnerable to climate shocks, with 21 million people living in rural areas – over 20% of them employed in agriculture, and more than one-third living below the poverty line. While dry and warm conditions in Central America are typical of El Niño events, current forecasts indicate a stronger-than-average El Niño in 2026, with higher temperatures and significantly reduced or irregular rainfall compared to past years. The effects of El Niño in 2026 may be particularly severe as they could affect both the primary and secondary crop seasons, leading to reduced maize, beans, and cash crop yields. Drought may also reduce the availability of water for domestic use, increasing the risk of unsafe water consumption. Above-average temperatures also raise the risk of heatwave events, posing significant public health concerns for at-risk populations, including children, elderly, pregnant women, and people with pre-existing medical conditions. ([NOAA 18/05/2026](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/analysis_monitoring/lanina/enso_evolution-status-fcsts-web.pdf), [IFRC 28/04/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/world/2026-super-el-nino-how-are-we-preparing-its-impact-latin-america-and-caribbean), [IRI accessed 27/04/2026](https://iri.columbia.edu/our-expertise/climate/forecasts/seasonal-climate-forecasts/), [WMO 24/04/2026](https://wmo.int/media/news/wmo-likelihood-increases-of-el-nino), [WMO accessed 27/04/2026](https://www.wmolc.org/seasonPmmeUI/view?winName=PlotView1777308240952), [FAO accessed 21/05/2026](https://www.fao.org/americas/priorities/central-american-dry-corridor/en))
hazard_materialisation: El Niño conditions and above-average temperatures are affecting Central America’s Dry Corridor, with particularly strong temperature evidence in El Salvador and Guatemala. El Niño conditions are forecast to strengthen during September–November, with a peak expected towards the end of 2026. In Honduras, there was a 100% probability of El Niño occurring during August–October, intensifying the mid-summer dry spell in late July and August and prompting drought alerts in 13 departments. In El Salvador, 14 temperature records were set in August, with temperatures reaching 43.9° C in Santa Rosa de Lima (La Unión Norte). Seasonal rainfall for August–November was forecast at 831.6mm, below the 939.0mm average, and a national red alert was declared on 25 August. In Guatemala, high temperatures caused rapid soil moisture loss, particularly in the Dry Corridor, where August rainfall reached only 5–25% of normal levels. In the Dry Corridor, farmers reported crop losses exceeding 50%, and some subsistence farmers reported losses of backyard poultry. No temperature data is available for Honduras, and the reported conditions do not establish direct attribution of specific impacts to El Niño. ([OCHA 22/09/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/honduras/honduras-llamamiento-urgente-sequia-sep-2026-resumen), [IPC 18/09/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/honduras/honduras-analisis-de-inseguridad-alimentaria-aguda-de-la-cif-agosto-octubre-2026-publicado-el-17-de-septiembre-de-2026), [Educo 04/09/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/el-salvador/educo-flash-update-and-appeal-1-el-salvador-meteorological-and-agricultural-drought-september-2026), [FEWS NET 18/09/2027](https://reliefweb.int/report/guatemala/guatemala-food-security-outlook-update-harvest-delays-and-losses-dry-corridor-will-prolong-market-dependence-august-2026-january-2027), [OCHA 01/10/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/guatemala/el-nino-2026-2027-climate-risk-humanitarian-outlook-latin-america-and-caribbean-september-2026))
impact_materialisation_description: El Niño-associated drought is increasing humanitarian needs across Central America’s Dry Corridor, particularly in food security, livelihoods, and WASH. In Honduras, WASH accounts for 708,000 people in need in red-alert municipalities, followed by food security and nutrition (622,000), health (617,000), and protection (400,000, including 80,000 targeted). Nationally, 1.88 million people are projected to face IPC 3 or worse between August–October. In Guatemala, the poorest households are likely to reduce food consumption and sell productive assets. Across 354 communities in El Salvador, Guatemala, and Honduras, 78.6% of maize-growing households reported crop losses of 75–100%, while 64.2% had maize reserves lasting three weeks or less. Agricultural employment has contracted sharply, particularly in El Salvador. Dehydration, child labour, family separation, and gender-based violence are additional anticipated concerns, although their impacts remain unquantified. ([OCHA 22/09/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/honduras/honduras-llamamiento-urgente-sequia-sep-2026-resumen), [IPC 18/09/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/honduras/honduras-analisis-de-inseguridad-alimentaria-aguda-de-la-cif-agosto-octubre-2026-publicado-el-17-de-septiembre-de-2026), [Educo 04/09/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/el-salvador/educo-flash-update-and-appeal-1-el-salvador-meteorological-and-agricultural-drought-september-2026), [FEWS NET 21/09/2027](https://reliefweb.int/report/guatemala/guatemala-food-security-outlook-update-harvest-delays-and-losses-dry-corridor-will-prolong-market-dependence-august-2026-january-2027), [OCHA 01/10/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/guatemala/el-nino-2026-2027-climate-risk-humanitarian-outlook-latin-america-and-caribbean-september-2026)).

title: Escalation of confrontation between Israel forces and Palestinian armed groups in the West Bank leads to increased displacement and livelihood and healthcare needs.
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale:
In April 2026, pressure on Palestinians in the West Bank notably intensified, with the monthly average of people displaced by lack-of-permit demolitions reaching 160, the highest monthly average recorded since 2009. In the largest single approval on record, Israeli authorities authorised 34 new settlements, bringing the total number of approvals under the current Government to 103. This pressure is compounded by movement restrictions, which reached 925 obstacles, the highest level in 20 years. These increased Israeli restrictions may drive conflict escalations between Israeli forces and Palestinian armed groups affiliated with Hamas.

Other triggers for escalations include the death penalty and related escalatory political discourse. On 30 March 2026, the Israeli Knesset passed a law mandating death by hanging for Palestinians convicted in military courts of carrying out deadly attacks against Israelis; the law could affect more than 9,300 Palestinian prisoners, and it has already triggered widespread Palestinian protests and strikes across the West Bank.

Following Israel’s adoption of this law, a Qassam Brigades spokesperson warned that attempts to impose executions would ignite broader confrontation. The spokesperson also called for intensified resistance in the West Bank, including individual “lone wolf” attacks and armed operations against Israeli forces. By late May, no such attacks had been reported, but the implementation of the law will likely trigger escalations of confrontations with Israeli forces and settlers.

Increased Israeli restrictions, annexations, and attempts to implement the death penalty law over the next three to six months will likely drive further clashes, shootings, and individual attacks. Hamas-affiliated cells, Palestinian Islamic Jihad fighters, and emerging regional armed groups such as the Jenin Brigade and Lions’ Den – particularly in East Jerusalem and Jenin, Nablus, and Tulkarem cities – are all likely to be involved in these escalations, which may include intensified Israeli raids, arrests, settler attacks, and movement restrictions around refugee camps, checkpoints, and settlements. ([OCHA 02/05/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/occupied-palestinian-territory/opt-humanitarian-situation-report-1-may-2026), [OCHA 24/04/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/occupied-palestinian-territory/opt-humanitarian-situation-report-23-april-2026), [ACLED 14/12/2023](https://acleddata.com/report/resurgence-armed-groups-west-bank-and-their-connections-gaza), [TNA 27/04/2026](https://www.newarab.com/analysis/encircling-jenin-how-israels-new-settlement-push-closing), [AA 30/03/2026](https://www.aa.com.tr/en/middle-east/israeli-knesset-passes-law-mandating-death-penalty-for-palestinian-prisoners/3885599), [AJ 01/04/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/4/1/palestinians-in-west-bank-protest-strike-against-israeli-death-penalty-law), [Samidoun 05/04/2026](https://samidoun.net/2026/04/abu-obeidas-statement-calls-for-widespread-action-to-defend-the-prisoners-and-al-aqsa/), [AJ 07/04/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/4/7/palestine-weekly-wrap-protests-sweep-west-bank-after-death-penalty-law))

title: Forecast El Niño conditions threaten crop production and worsen food insecurity in Kenya
rationale:
El Niño conditions are forecast to develop by July 2026 and strengthen through the second half of the year. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration estimates a 61% probability of El Niño from May–July, rising to 87–92% between July 2026 and January 2027. The Intergovernmental Authority on Development Climate Prediction and Applications Centre forecasts below-normal June–September (JJAS) rainfall across western and northern Kenya alongside above-normal temperatures nationwide, closely resembling the 2023 El Niño, when below-normal JJAS rainfall affected western Kenya.
The forecast threatens Kenya's principal food-producing areas during a critical stage of the long rains season. Over 70% of the country's annual crop production depends on the long rains, which extend into August–September in the North Rift and western Kenya. These areas had already recorded below-average rainfall in April and early May despite favourable national rainfall totals. Combined with delayed fertiliser deliveries, below-average rainfall and above-average temperatures from June–September are likely to reduce yields of maize, beans, sorghum, and sweet potato, resulting in a below-average October–November harvest.
In northern and eastern pastoral areas, above-average temperatures during the June–September dry season are expected to accelerate the deterioration of rangeland and water resources. Recovery remains fragile after the 2020–2023 drought and the 2023–2024 floods, with depleted herd sizes, persistent livestock disease, and reduced vaccination programmes limiting resilience.
The deteriorating production outlook comes as maize and bean prices remain 6–21% and 8–17% above the five-year average, respectively, driven by depleted household stocks following the poor 2025 short rains, high transport costs, and strong market demand. High household debt further constrains purchasing power. A below-average harvest would tighten domestic food supplies, drive prices higher, and further reduce incomes and food access for farming and pastoral households. ([ICPAC 19/05/2026](https://www.icpac.net/news/drier-than-usual-conditions-with-warmer-than-average-temperatures-expected-in-the-greater-horn-of-africa/), [GEOGLAM Crop Monitor 02/04/2026](https://www.cropmonitor.org/crop-monitor-for-early-warning), [FEWS NET 04/06/2026](https://fews.net/east-africa/kenya/key-message-update/may-2026-0), [FEWS NET 07/05/2026](https://fews.net/east-africa/kenya/food-security-outlook-update/april-2026), [NDMA 14/04/2026](https://ndma.go.ke/drought-situation-brief/), [IPC 21/03/2026](https://www.ipcinfo.org/ipc-country-analysis/details-map/en/c/1159540/), [FEWS NET accessed 08/07/2026](https://fews.net/sites/default/files/2024-07/KE-Seasonal-Calendar-202406.pdf))

Description: 
Climate forecasts indicate a high and rising likelihood of El Niño conditions developing during May–July 2026, strengthening through the second half of the year. ICPAC's May 2026 forecast points to a high probability of below-normal JJAS rainfall across western and northern Kenya — where the unimodal long rains season in fact extends into August/September and has already tracked below average in April and early May — alongside above-normal temperatures. This combination is expected to reduce soil moisture during the critical grain-filling and maturation stages of long rains crops in the North Rift and western Kenya, directly threatening the October–November harvest. Title: El Niño raises risk of flooding during the October–December short rains season in eastern and coastal Kenya
Description: 
El Niño conditions are historically associated with enhanced rainfall during Kenya's October–December short rains season, particularly across eastern and coastal areas. During the 2023 El Niño, wetter-than-normal OND conditions across eastern Kenya materialised as severe and damaging flooding. With seasonal forecast anticipating high probability of above-average precipitation between October and December 2026, a comparable pattern of enhanced short rains is likely. This risk may also be compounded by the positive condition of the Indian Ocean Dipole, expected to start from August-September, which typically enhances the effects of El Nino in eastern Africa. Should this materialise, flooding would damage infrastructure and cropland in areas already weakened by successive climate shocks, further compounding humanitarian needs heading into early 2027.

title: Forecast below-average Kiremt rains in Ethiopia threaten food production and livelihoods
rationale:
El Niño conditions are forecast to develop by July 2026 and strengthen through the second half of the year. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration puts the probability of El Niño from May–July at around 61%, rising to 87–92% between July 2026 and January 2027. The Intergovernmental Authority on Development Climate Prediction and Applications Centre's May 2026 forecast indicates a high likelihood of below-normal June–September Kiremt rainfall across Ethiopia, with above-normal temperatures. Severe localised deficits are likely in the northeast and central areas, with at least 50% probability of deficits reaching 50% or more.
Kiremt is the primary rainy season for Ethiopia's northern and central cropping areas, governing the Meher harvest – the country's most important crop season, which produces the most teff, maize, sorghum, wheat, and barley across Amhara, Central Ethiopia, Oromia, the Southern regions, and Tigray. Below-average rainfall would cut yields and household food production. In Tigray and Amhara, poor rains may also reduce agricultural labour income during the June–August lean season.
In past El Niño episodes, Meher maize and sorghum production fell across Ethiopia, most sharply in eastern Amhara,  northeastern Oromia, and Tigray; national yields dropped by around 2% below normal, with localised deficits of 10–15%. High fertiliser and fuel prices will likely limit farmers' input use during planting, lowering yield potential even with adequate rainfall, while raising transport costs for inputs and produce.
Staple food prices are already exceptionally high; annual food inflation reached 13.5% in April, up from 11% in March but down from 15.6% in April 2025 – a renewed monthly acceleration after disinflation, not a sustained year-on-year worsening. Drivers include increased fuel costs from Middle East conflict-linked energy disruptions, seasonal lean season food supply tightening, and trade disruptions, which are severely straining poor rural households.
El Niño typically also boosts the October–December rainfall across lowland/riverine eastern East Africa. Forecasts show a very high chance of above-average rainfall across central and eastern Ethiopia, likely driving flooding in flood-prone lowlands. ([ICPAC 19/05/2026](https://www.icpac.net/news/drier-than-usual-conditions-with-warmer-than-average-temperatures-expected-in-the-greater-horn-of-africa/), [FEWS NET 03/06/2026](https://fews.net/east-africa/ethiopia/key-message-update/may-2026), [FEWS NET 10/03/2026](https://fews.net/east-africa/ethiopia/food-security-outlook/february-2026), [FEWS NET 18/05/2026](https://fews.net/east-africa/seasonal-monitor/may-2026), [GEOGLAM Crop Monitor 02/06/2026](https://www.cropmonitor.org/crop-monitor-for-amis), [WMO accessed 08/07/2026](wmolc.org/seasonPmmeUI/view?winName=PlotView1781162850270))

Title: Strengthening El Niño raises risk of flooding during the October–December season in lowland and riverine areas of Ethiopia
Description: 
El Niño conditions are historically associated with enhanced rainfall during the October–December season across eastern East Africa. With seasonal forecast anticipating high probability of above-average precipitation between October and December 2026, there is an increased likelihood of flooding across flood-prone lowland areas of Ethiopia, especially the Somali Region. This risk may also be compounded by the positive condition of the Indian Ocean Dipole, expected to start from August-September, which typically enhances the effects of El Nino in eastern Africa.

title: El Niño drives drought conditions, increasing food insecurity and heightening humanitarian needs in Madagascar in 2027
rationale: Current models indicate a very high probability for El Niño to develop by July 2026 and persist into early 2027. In Madagascar, El Niño typically drives precipitation and temperature anomalies, with dry conditions in southern parts of the country and heavy rainfall in the north and east. In 2015–2016 and 2023–2024, El Niño caused prolonged drought conditions and crop failure, resulting in increased food insecurity that particularly affected the country's south. Seasonal forecasts anticipate near-average precipitation in July–September and below-average precipitation across most of the country in October–December. The same forecasts indicate a very high probability of above-average temperatures across the entire country in July–December. Drier and hotter-than-average conditions may affect the start of the rainy season, which runs October–April and is essential for producing Madagascar's main staple cereals, such as maize and rice, harvested in April–June. This may lead to below-average yields, with severe consequences for the population's access to food in 2027, widening food consumption gaps and increasing malnutrition rates. Impacts may also extend to other staple crops, such as cassava, beans, and sweet potatoes, as well as to agricultural labour availability, which usually peaks between November–March. Limited rainfall and abnormally high temperatures may also reduce pasture availability, resulting in deteriorating livestock body conditions and increased morbidity and mortality. Dry conditions are also likely to affect access to water for domestic consumption, potentially leading to reliance on unsafe water sources and limiting hygiene and sanitation practices. These combined effects are expected to increase humanitarian needs, strain local coping mechanisms, and heighten dependence on external assistance, particularly among rural households already vulnerable to climate variability. The country shows a high pre-existing vulnerability to climatic shocks, including reliance on rainfed agriculture, limited water and sanitation infrastructure, and low coping capacity. ([Moov 03/06/2026](https://www.moov.mg/actualite/nationale/116639-el-nino-est-de-retour-quel-impact-pour-madagascar#body2), [WMO 02/06/2026](https://public.wmo.int/news/media-centre/wmo-prepare-el-nino), [NewsMada 08/06/2026](https://newsmada.com/2026/06/03/el-nino-sinvite-en-hiver-madagascar-sous-la-menace-dune-nouvelle-secheresse/), [FEWS NET 05/06/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/madagascar/madagascar-key-message-update-severe-rainfall-deficits-reduce-agricultural-yields-southwestern-madagascar-may-september-2026), [FEWS NET accessed 12/06/2026](https://fews.net/southern-africa/madagascar), [EU 08/06/2026](https://joint-research-centre.ec.europa.eu/jrc-news-and-updates/agricultural-production-threatened-combination-el-nino-and-high-input-prices-2026-06-08_en), [UNRIC 21/04/2026](https://unric.org/en/madagascar-one-of-the-countries-most-exposed-to-climate-extremes/), [UNDRR 12/06/2026](https://www.preventionweb.net/resource/case-study/anticipatory-action-drought-southern-madagascar-calibrating-trigger-systems), [WMO accessed 15/06/2026](https://wmolc.org/seasonPmmeUI/plot_PMME#))

title: El Niño-induced dry conditions in southern and central Mozambique and floods in the northern provinces increase humanitarian needs in 2026 and early 2027
rationale: Climate projections indicate a high likelihood of El Niño conditions developing in July 2026 and persisting into the 2026/2027 rainy season, coinciding with Mozambique's main agricultural period. El Niño will drive contrasting rainfall patterns, with drier conditions in southern and central regions and wetter conditions in the north. The anticipated event is driven by abnormal warming of equatorial Pacific sea surface temperatures, which disrupts global atmospheric circulation and rainfall patterns. El Niño typically brings below-normal rains in southern Mozambique and above-normal rains to the northern provinces, raising the likelihood of flooding and river overflow. Seasonal forecasts for the October–December period anticipate these typical El Niño patterns, indicating a moderate probability of above-average precipitation in the north and below-average precipitation in the south. The entire country is expected to experience above-average temperatures in July–December, which will compound dry conditions in the south and increase the risk of waterborne and vector-borne diseases in flood-exposed areas. Mozambique's high exposure to climate variability and reliance on rainfed agriculture further amplify vulnerability to climatic shocks. From September–October 2026, delayed or below-average precipitation in southern and central areas, combined with abnormally high temperatures, may affect land preparation and planting. If dry conditions continue through early 2027, crop yields and water availability may decrease, leading to a below-average maize, rice, millet, and sorghum harvest. At the same time, northern areas are likely to experience above-average precipitation, which may be beneficial to agriculture but also increases the risk of flooding, infrastructure damage, and displacement. These combined impacts are expected to increase humanitarian needs, particularly in food security, nutrition, WASH, and health. ([WMO 02/06/2026](https://wmo.int/news/media-centre/wmo-prepare-el-nino), [FEWS NET accessed 11/06/2026]( https://fews.net/southern-africa/mozambique), [CoM 18/05/2026](https://clubofmozambique.com/news/mozambique-inam-warns-el-nino-may-affect-key-sectors/), [WMO 24/04/2026] (https://wmo.int/media/news/wmo-likelihood-increases-of-el-nino), [Noticias 16/05/2026](https://www.noticiasaominuto.com/economia/2990923/mocambique-em-alerta-face-a-nova-previsao-de-um-evento-el-nino-forte), [Afroline 17/05/2026](https://afroline.co.mz/2026/05/mocambique-alerta-el-nino-2026-2027-ameaca-agravamento-de-secas-e-inundacoes/), [FEWS NET 21/05/2026](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/international/FEWS_REPORT/Mozambique/Current.pdf))

Trigger ID: R1047 - T0628
Title: Below-average rainfall and rising temperatures in southern and central regions
Description: 
Below-average rainfall and rising temperatures in southern and central regions: 
During El Niño events, large-scale atmospheric circulation shifts suppress moisture transport into southern Africa, reducing rainfall during the main cropping season. In southern and central Mozambique, this often results in prolonged dry spells, erratic rainfall distribution, and early cessation of rains rather than a complete absence of precipitation. At the same time, above-average temperatures increase evapotranspiration rates, accelerating the loss of soil moisture and surface water. This combination reduces water availability for domestic consumption, crops and livestock, heightens the risk of pasture degradation, and can lead to reduced agricultural yields or crop failure, particularly for rainfed smallholder farmers.
Sources: 
(Afroline 17/05/2026 ; CoM 18/05/2026 ; FEWS NET 21/05/2026 ; WMO 02/06/2026 ; IRI accessed 11/06/2026)

Trigger ID: R1047 - T0629
Title: Above-average rainfall in northern provinces
Description: 
El Niño conditions can enhance moisture inflow in parts of northern Mozambique, leading to above-average and more intense rainfall events. This increases the likelihood of river overflow, flash floods, and waterlogging, especially in low-lying and flood-prone districts. Saturated soils reduce infiltration and increase surface runoff, amplifying flood severity even during short periods of heavy rainfall. Flooding can damage homes, crops, and transport infrastructure, disrupt market access, and increase the risk of population displacement and waterborne diseases, further compounding humanitarian needs.
Sources: 
(Afroline 17/05/2026 ; CoM 18/05/2026 ; FEWS NET 21/05/2026 ; WMO 02/06/2026)

Trigger ID: R1047 - T0630
Title: Delayed onset and irregular distribution of rains
Description: 
El Niño is often associated with a late or erratic start to the rainy season, followed by uneven rainfall patterns throughout the season. In Mozambique, this disrupts the agricultural calendar, delaying planting and reducing the effective growing period for key crops such as maize. Intermittent dry spells during critical crop growth stages can further reduce yields. At the same time, unpredictable rainfall undermines farmers’ decision-making and increases the likelihood of replanting, leading to higher input costs and reduced resilience among households dependent on farming.
Sources: 
(Afroline 17/05/2026 ; CoM 18/05/2026 ; FEWS NET 21/05/2026 ; WMO 02/06/2026)

title: RSF expansion in Blue Nile state triggers displacement and protection risks
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale:
The RSF offensive launched in early 2026 against Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) positions in Baw county opened a new front in Blue Nile state. This has significantly increased the likelihood of conflict spreading to previously unaffected areas to the north, particularly Ed Damazine, the state capital, as well as the strategic corridor leading to the Roseires Dam. By advancing in Blue Nile state, RSF seeks to strengthen its position to recapture and control central Sudan, later opening a route through Sennar state. 
Following heavy territorial losses in 2025, including entire states in central Sudan, RSF has reconstituted its operational capacity through its alliance with Abdelaziz Adam al Hilu's Sudan People's Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N/Al Hilu). Access to terrain under its control has provided RSF with defensive depth, cross-border supply lines, and logistical continuity. This enables it to sustain multifront operations and power its advance in Blue Nile, positioning the RSF for a prolonged and expanded offensive rather than a short-term tactical push and increasing the likelihood of escalation beyond the current front lines.
External facilitation further compounds these dynamics. SAF has repeatedly accused South Sudan and Ethiopia of enabling this mobilisation, with satellite imagery from February 2026 showing a logistics camp near the Ethiopian border in Benishangul Gumz despite official Ethiopian denial. If sustained, such external support would significantly raise the possibility of a scaled-up offensive by insulating RSF operations from battlefield setbacks ([ACLED 26/01/2026](https://acleddata.com/report/blue-nile-peripheral-front-central-battleground-sudan-conflict ), [MEE 26/01/2026](https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/sudans-rsf-launches-offensive-blue-nile-state), [AJ 19/08/2025](https://www.aljazeera.com/features/longform/2025/8/19/inside-the-nuba-mountains-and-the-alliance-reshaping-sudans-civil-war ), [ACLED 15/04/2025](https://acleddata.com/report/two-years-war-sudan-how-saf-gaining-upper-hand), [ICG 07/04/2025](https://www.crisisgroup.org/stm/africa/sudan/two-years-sudans-war-spreading), [Reuters 10/02/2026](https://www.reuters.com/investigations/ethiopia-builds-secret-camp-train-sudan-rsf-fighters-sources-say-2026-02-10/ ), [ST 25/01/2026](https://sudantribune.com/article/309824))

title: RSF restoration of siege on Al Obeid, North Kordofan drives widescale displacement towards White Nile state
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale:
Since October 2025, RSF has mobilised troops near Al Obeid's borders, including deploying combat vehicles along the western side. The sustained mobilisation and positioning of these forces indicate preparation for a renewed offensive to reinstate a siege of the city. A previous siege of the city between May 2023 and February 2025 demonstrated RSF's operational ability to isolate Al Obeid for prolonged periods, resulting in a significant deterioration in humanitarian conditions, including severe food insecurity.
RSF has a strong strategic incentive to restore the siege because of Al Obeid's role as a key logistic and commercial hub linking western and southern Sudan to Khartoum and central Sudan. Control of the city would provide RSF with greater leverage over supply routes, trade flows, and access to corridors into SAF-controlled areas, particularly central Sudan. Al Obeid's role as a major crop and livestock market and a gate for Kordofan exports further increases its strategic and economic importance to RSF.
Despite recent SAF advancements and repositioning in North Kordofan, fluid conflict dynamics and continued shifts in areas of control between SAF and RSF increase the likelihood of renewed attempts to siege the city over the next six months. This likelihood is further reinforced by increasing logistical and technical support provided to RSF by the United Arab Emirates (UAE), which may improve the group's operational capacity to sustain offensive and siege tactics. ([UN 19/12/2025](https://news.un.org/en/story/2025/12/1166633), [Darfur24 13/11/2025](https://www.darfur24.com/en/2025/11/13/military-document-reveals-rsf-preparations-for-major-attack-on-el-obeid/), [YSPH HRL 16/01/2026](https://files-profile.medicine.yale.edu/documents/8dce0cc5-35fb-4078-b2aa-748e51cc8e9d), [BBC 06/01/2026](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c74w54783zeo), [Sudan War Monitor 24/02/2025](https://sudanwarmonitor.com/p/sudan-army-breaks-rsf-siege-of-el), [OHCHR 19/09/2025](https://www.ohchr.org/en/documents/country-reports/human-rights-situation-sudan-1-january-30-june-2025), [MEE 24/02/2025](https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/sudans-army-breaks-rsf-siege-strategic-city-el-obeid), [The National 09/12/2025](https://www.thenationalnews.com/news/mena/2025/12/09/al-obeid-gripped-by-fear-as-sudans-army-and-rsf-square-off-for-fierce-battle/), [AJ 14/11/2025](https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2025/11/14/will-sudans-rsf-turn-strategic-city-of-el-obeid-into-another-el-fasher), [TNH 29/04/2026](https://www.thenewhumanitarian.org/analysis/2026/04/29/how-sudan-el-obeid-survives-drone-strikes-siege-warfare), [AJ 06/03/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/3/6/sudanese-army-retakes-bara-secures-el-obeid-in-north-kordofan), [Le Monde 22/03/2026](https://www.lemonde.fr/en/le-monde-africa/article/2026/03/22/the-uae-is-reorganizing-its-arms-supply-network-for-sudanese-paramilitaries_6751682_124.html), [DW 13/02/2026](https://www.dw.com/en/sudan-civil-war-ethiopias-uaes-role-under-scrutiny/a-75913225), [TRT World 21/02/2026](https://www.trtworld.com/article/e24ea66b0dc2))

title: Interregional trade restrictions disrupt markets and deepen food insecurity in West Kordofan
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale: The continuation or expansion of trade bans imposed in late 2025 by Khartoum, Northern, and North Kordofan states on the movement of goods into RSF-controlled areas would likely further restrict supplies to West Kordofan. These restrictions would affect food, fuel, medicines, agricultural inputs, and other essential commodities. West Kordofan is particularly exposed because it is landlocked and has historically depended on supply chains from northern and eastern Sudan, including routes through Khartoum, Red Sea ports, and Egypt. As formal routes become more restricted, markets are likely to rely increasingly on informal supply routes that are longer, more insecure, and more expensive because of checkpoints, unofficial taxation, transport delays, and insecurity. Alternative routes through Al Na'am market near Abyei provide some supply capacity but are limited and vulnerable to shocks, including fires, border tensions, and armed-party interference. If bans persist, supply shortages and price increases are likely to deepen food insecurity and market fragmentation across the state. title: A rift between SAF and allied groups in Khartoum leads to worsening humanitarian conditions and protection concerns
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale: The Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) face growing pressure from key external allies, including Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and the US, to distance itself from allied armed groups with political Islam leanings, including the Al Baraa Bin Malik Brigade. This creates a risk of fragmentation within SAF's alliance structure, as attempts to contain, integrate, or undermine these groups could provoke resistance. SAF remains operationally dependent on allied armed groups for manpower, mobilisation, funding channels, and battlefield capacity across multiple fronts, making coercive integration difficult. Tensions have also emerged between SAF and factions linked to JEM, the Joint Forces, and other groups present in civilian and commercial areas in Khartoum. US designation and sanctions linked to the Sudanese Muslim Brotherhood and Al Baraa Bin Malik Brigade add further external pressure on SAF to disengage from these groups. If SAF pursues integration or restrictions while these actors retain military leverage and local positions, tensions could escalate into localised clashes, checkpoint competition, and fragmented territorial control in Khartoum and central Sudan. title: Long-range RSF drones targeting the eastern supply corridor and Port Sudan disrupt trade and aid delivery in Red Sea state
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale: RSF tactics have increasingly shifted from ground offensives in SAF-controlled areas to long-range drone strikes. The May 2025 strikes on Port Sudan's fuel reservoirs demonstrated RSF's capacity to hit locations far from its main areas of control using long-range kamikaze drones. Port Sudan remains a strategic target because it continues to host key government, technical, and logistical functions, while the Port Sudan-Kassala-Gedaref corridor remains central to Sudan's economy and humanitarian response. Before the conflict, this corridor handled most international trade, and it continues to support imports, fuel supplies, and humanitarian cargo entering SAF-controlled areas. Targeting the corridor would allow RSF to undermine SAF supply chains and disrupt commercial and aid flows without needing to control territory in eastern Sudan. The likelihood of more frequent or damaging attacks would increase if RSF receives sustained external support, expands cross-border supply networks, or gains greater long-range drone capacity. Regional tensions around the Red Sea may further increase the corridor's strategic sensitivity. ([Reuters 12/09/2025](https://www.reuters.com/investigations/how-sudans-rsf-used-drones-its-civil-war-2025-09-12/), [Milton et al. 09/11/2025](https://ctc.westpoint.edu/sudans-long-range-drone-war/), [UN 18/01/2026](https://news.un.org/en/story/2026/01/1166786), [EPC 08/09/2023](https://epc.ae/en/details/scenario/port-sudan-the-economics-and-geopolitics-of-sudans-new-capital), [ACAPS 23/05/2025](https://www.acaps.org/en/countries/archives/detail/sudan-risk-of-continued-drone-strikes-on-port-sudan), [Le Monde 22/03/2026](https://www.lemonde.fr/en/le-monde-africa/article/2026/03/22/the-uae-is-reorganizing-its-arms-supply-network-for-sudanese-paramilitaries_6751682_124.html))

title: RSF drone attacks damage the Merowe Dam and power grid in Northern state, disrupting health, food security, and public services
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale: Since 2025, RSF has expanded its long-range drone capabilities, including kamikaze munitions able to target infrastructure far inside SAF-controlled areas. Northern and River Nile states have already experienced repeated drone attacks on infrastructure, including strikes affecting Merowe Dam and associated power facilities. These attacks have mostly caused temporary disruptions rather than sustained structural damage, but they demonstrate intent and reach. The risk would increase if SAF-RSF fighting intensifies and RSF continues receiving external support that improves its long-range strike capacity. RSF has a clear strategic incentive to target Merowe Dam because it is Sudan's largest hydroelectric dam and supports electricity generation, irrigation, and economic activity across areas under SAF control. Disrupting the dam or the associated electricity grid would allow RSF to increase pressure on SAF governance, undermine public confidence, and disrupt services in areas away from front lines. While imminent large-scale escalation in Northern state is not clearly indicated, the dam's strategic importance makes damaging attacks a credible medium-term risk. title: Mass returns from eastern Chad exacerbate humanitarian needs in West Darfur State
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale: Deteriorating humanitarian conditions, aid shortfalls, and insecurity in eastern Chad are increasingly pushing Sudanese refugees to return to unsafe areas in Darfur, particularly West Darfur. Return movements rose in early 2026, with April arrivals into West Darfur nearly doubling compared with November 2025 levels. Many returnees cited access to resources, services, and humanitarian assistance as a main driver, suggesting that deteriorating conditions in displacement are influencing return decisions. Funding cuts and reduced assistance in Chad have weakened refugee coping capacity and strained already overstretched refugee-hosting areas. Planned relocations away from the Sudan border, following RSF cross-border attacks and Chadian military deployment, may increase uncertainty and pressure on some households to return prematurely. Political instability and tensions within Chad, including dynamics linked to alleged external support for RSF and tensions among groups affected by violence in Darfur, could make refugee-hosting areas less predictable. These factors may increase unsafe returns to Darfur despite continuing insecurity, limited services, and protection risks. title: Resource-related clashes and political tensions in Tindouf camps restrict humanitarian access and increase protection risks for Sahrawi refugees
rationale:
The risk of increased instability and localised clashes in the Sahrawi refugee camps in Tindouf, Algeria, may rise over the coming months as humanitarian pressures, political uncertainty, and governance challenges compound a protracted displacement crisis.  

Several incidents between April–June 2026 suggest growing tensions within the camps. On 20 April, armed confrontations involving Polisario-linked elements and the Algerian National Army over humanitarian aid distribution highlighted tensions related to influence, compounded by the lack of resources. On 28 April, clashes between members of the Fakra and Oulad Moussa tribes in Smara camp escalated from a dispute over access to a water tap into armed confrontations involving live ammunition. The violence resulted in injuries and damage to tents, houses, and vehicles, raising concerns about the capacity of camp authorities to manage local disputes and prevent escalation. 

In this context, tensions are most likely to unfold through repeated, low-level disputes between tribes, families, or Polisario-affiliated actors in camps such as Smara, Laayoune, Awserd, and Dakhla, particularly around water points, aid distribution systems, and local administrative structures. These disputes are likely to remain contained but may escalate into short-lived violent incidents when mediation fails or when armed actors become involved. 

Political developments have further increased uncertainty and may be contributing to growing confusion and frustration among refugee populations regarding future governance arrangements. On 22 April, reports indicated increased US pressure on Algeria regarding the future of the Tindouf camps and the Western Sahara conflict. On 29 May, concerns emerged among Polisario supporters over a perceived shift in Algeria's position on negotiations. On 9 June, the death of senior Polisario commander Lahbib Mohamed Abdelaziz in a reported drone strike fuelled speculation regarding future leadership dynamics within the movement. 

Although these developments have not triggered widespread unrest, they indicate increasing pressure on camp governance, resource management, and political cohesion. Further reductions in humanitarian assistance, deterioration in living conditions, or renewed political tensions surrounding Western Sahara could increase the likelihood of additional intercommunal violence, protests, or localised instability within the camps over the next 6–12 months. ([ACLED accessed 18/06/2026](https://acleddata.com/conflict-data/data-export-tool\), [UNHCR 27/11/2025](https://algeria.un.org/fr/306201-plan-de-r%C3%A9ponse-pour-les-r%C3%A9fugi%C3%A9s-sahraouis-2026%E2%80%932027\), [Africanews 23/04/2026](https://www.africanews.com/2026/04/23/in-algerian-desert-sahrawi-refugees-still-dream-of-independent-homeland/), [Atalayar 22/04/2026](https://www.atalayar.com/en/articulo/politics/the-united-states-is-putting-pressure-on-algeria-and-urging-it-to-dismantle-the-tindouf-camps/20260422210000225067.html), [Algeria Times 20/04/2026](https://algeriatimes.net/detail/view/75054\), [Yabiladi 29/04/2026](https://en.yabiladi.com/articles/details/193455/violent-clashes-tindouf-s-smara-camp.html\), [Barlaman Today 30/04/2026](https://barlamantoday.com/2026/04/30/deadly-armed-clashes-reportedly-erupt-in-tindouf-camps/), [Assahifa 29/05/2026](https://www.assahifa.com/%D8%B9%D9%82%D8%A8-%D8%BA%D8%B6%D8%A8-%D9%85%D8%AE%D9%8A%D9%85%D8%A7%D8%AA-%D8%AA%D9%86%D8%AF%D9%88%D9%81-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%AC%D8%B2%D8%A7%D8%A6%D8%B1-%D8%AA%D8%AD%D8%A7%D9%88%D9%84-%D8%B7%D9%85%D8%A3/), [Algeria Times 11/06/2026](https://algeriatimes.net/detail/view/75662\), [Belpresse 09/06/2026](https://www.belpresse.com/politique/%d9%85%d9%82%d8%aa%d9%84-%d9%86%d8%ac%d9%84-%d8%a7%d9%84%d8%b2%d8%b9%d9%8a%d9%85-%d8%a7%d9%84%d8%b3%d8%a7%d8%a8%d9%82-%d9%84%d9%84%d8%a8%d9%88%d9%84%d9%8a%d8%b3%d8%a7%d8%b1%d9%8a%d9%88-%d9%8a%d8%b6/)).
hazard_materialisation: The risk's hazard materialised, but the anticipated impact did not. The hazard was evident in August, with an armed clash within the Polisario Front on 7 August and two peaceful protests on 15 August over detainee treatment and perceived unequal access to medical evacuation. These developments were consistent with the risk's anticipated resource-related and political tensions. In September, pressure remained evident, including allegations of mismanagement in medical evacuations, while political pressure around the Tindouf camps continued, including Morocco's 9 September call for durable solutions and Spain's 10 September approval of a nationality bill potentially affecting Sahrawis. Despite this, the anticipated humanitarian impact – major disruption to aid distribution, water, health services, or camp administration – did not materialise. ACLED recorded no fatalities from the August incidents, and the monitoring does not indicate significant disruption to humanitarian operations or large-scale displacement. title: El Niño-driven agricultural losses and water shortages in the Philippines increase food security, WASH, and health needs
rationale:
The Philippines faces an increasing risk of El Niño-driven drought, potentially triggering water shortages, agricultural losses, and heat stress in the coming months. El Niño conditions are already present in the tropical Pacific, with sea surface temperature anomalies reaching the +0.5° C threshold in May 2026; most models indicate an over 80% probability of full development, persisting until early 2027 at strong to very strong intensity.
Seasonal forecasts anticipate below-average precipitation across central and southern regions from July–September, extending nationwide from October. The provinces likely to be affected are Abra, Apayao, Benguet, Ifugao, Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur, Isabela, Kalinga, La Union, Mountain Province, Nueva Ecija, Nueva Vizcaya, Pangasinan, Quirino, and Tarlac. Temperatures are forecast above seasonal averages nationwide from July–December. This is likely to produce a poor monsoon season (May–October), vital for maize and rice production, affecting both rain-fed and irrigated crops. Main season rice, harvested in December, accounts for 60% of domestic production.
The Philippines has experienced 12 major drought events since 1968. It is estimated that agricultural drought caused approximately 20 million metric tons of crop losses between 1980–2020. Between July 2023 and April 2024, El Niño-related dry conditions affected multiple provinces, causing agricultural losses, water shortages, and livelihood disruptions. The Department of Social Welfare and Development reported thousands of farming households affected by prolonged dry spells, with losses in some provinces reaching hundreds of millions of pesos. This event also drove extreme heat, school disruptions, and mounting pressure on water and food systems – illustrating how El Niño can rapidly become a multisector humanitarian crisis for affected communities.
In the next one to three months, primary concerns include localised rainfall deficits, water stress, and heat-related impacts, particularly in affected agricultural zones. Over the next three to six months, if El Niño strengthens as projected, drought conditions could intensify significantly, leading to reduced crop yields, livestock stress, water shortages, rising food prices, and worsening livelihood pressures. This may increase humanitarian needs in the WASH, food security, and health sectors, particularly in already-vulnerable rural communities. ([PAGASA accessed 17/06/2026](https://www.pagasa.dost.gov.ph/climate/el-nino-la-nina/monitoring), [PIA 05/06/2026](https://pia.gov.ph/news/el-nino-to-emerge-in-june-intensify-into-strong-to-very-strong-condition-by-year-end-pagasa/), [FAO accessed 17/06/2026](https://www.fao.org/in-action/drought-portal/preparedness/vulnerability-and-impact-assessment/national-case-studies/the-philippines-case/en), [WB accessed 17/06/2026](https://climateknowledgeportal.worldbank.org/country/philippines/enso), [GMA 26/04/2026](https://www.gmanetwork.com/news/weather/content/985366/drought-philippines-2026/story/))
triggers_raw:
Trigger ID: R1058 - T0655
Title: Below-average rainfall and above-average temperatures
Description: 
El Niño typically suppresses rainfall across the Philippines while also contributing to above-average temperatures. During the monsoon season, it also contributes to irregular rainfall distribution, characterized by intermittent dry spells and uneven precipitation.  Reduced or unheavenly distributed rainfall, combined with high temperatures, increases evapotranspiration, accelerating the depletion of soil moisture, while reduced precipitation affect surface and groundwater reserves. This can significantly reduce water availability for domestic consumption, irrigation, and livestock, particularly in drought-prone and agriculture-dependent provinces. Prolonged heat and moisture stress can also damage crops during critical growth stages, reduce agricultural productivity, and increase heat-related health risks, especially among affected rural households and outdoor workers.
Sources: 
([PAGASA Accessed 17/06/2026](https://www.pagasa.dost.gov.ph/climate/el-nino-la-nina/monitoring); [PIA 05/06/2026](https://pia.gov.ph/news/el-nino-to-emerge-in-june-intensify-into-strong-to-very-strong-condition-by-year-end-pagasa/); [FAO accessed 17/06/2026](https://www.fao.org/in-action/drought-portal/preparedness/vulnerability-and-impact-assessment/national-case-studies/the-philippines-case/en))

title: Peace talk end and military offensive against armed groups in Colombia escalate conflict and increase civilian casualties and displacement
rationale:
After the elections in June 2026, Abelardo de la Espriella’s win as Colombia's new President signalled a major change in the country's stance towards non-state armed groups (NSAGs) and drug trafficking organisations. The President-elect has since announced an end to peace negotiations and a nationwide military offensive to begin once he takes office on 7 August, including a 90-day security crackdown involving military deployments, aerial operations, and coca eradication measures.
This shift may increase the risk of clashes, civilian casualties, displacement, and confinement, particularly in Pacific Coast departments, including Cauca, Chocó, Nariño, and Valle del Cauca, as well as in Norte de Santander and Putumayo, which were among Colombia’s most conflict-affected areas in 2025.
This risk is compounded by the significant strengthening of NSAGs in recent years. Armed group membership has grown substantially since 2022. Armed groups have simultaneously expanded into new territories, adopted new warfare tactics, including the use of explosive drones, and extended social control against communities, including curfews and checkpoints. Ahead of the anticipated offensive, NSAGs are expected to intensify operations to consolidate territorial control, while retaliatory actions during the crackdown could further increase civilian harm. In response, the elected President has proposed Plan Colombia 2.0, aimed at recovering NSAG-controlled territory, eradicating coca cultivation and illegal mining (the primary financing sources for armed groups), and securing record investment in state armed forces, with the political and financial support of the US Government.
As a result, July, the month preceding the new Government's inauguration, is expected to see an intensification of NSAG violence as armed groups seek to consolidate territorial control and prepare ahead of the anticipated military offensive. Over the first 90-day period (August–October), a marked increase in armed clashes with state forces is expected, a trend that should persist throughout the remainder of 2026. These dynamics will directly affect civilian populations in the departments highlighted, where most rural and Indigenous communities reside.
Planned government reforms, including major cuts to state bureaucracy and measures targeting officials linked to the previous administration, could also increase political tensions and trigger social mobilisation, adding a civil unrest dimension to the risk.
A historic ‘Super El Niño’ event, forecast to intensify through late 2026, is expected to compound these dynamics. Authorities are warning of extreme heat, drought, and water shortages, with national implications for food security. This adds further pressure on communities in the departments covered by this risk, where access to food is already constrained by confinement and mobility restrictions linked to armed group activity.

title: Permanent military exclusion zone east of the Yellow Line before the Israeli elections increases displacement and humanitarian access constraints
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale:
There is a high probability that Israeli forces will formally declare and physically enclose a permanent military exclusion zone east of the Yellow Line in the period leading up to Israel's October 2026 parliamentary elections, progressively reducing the territory accessible to civilians and humanitarian responders.
Since the 10 October 2025 ceasefire, Israeli forces have steadily expanded their military footprint beyond the initial demarcation line through tank advances, repeated evacuation orders, the construction of defensive positions, and localised operations. The Israeli-controlled area had expanded from 53% of Gaza Strip at the ceasefire to 64.9% by June 2026, with the trend notably intensifying late into the month. The Armed Conflict Location & Event Data reports that events reflecting Yellow Line expansion and associated military movements increased from an average of fewer than four events per month between October 2025 and mid-June 2026 to 22 events between 18 June and 17 July 2026, a more than fivefold increase.

During the same period, activity by the Shuja’iyya Popular Defense Forces led by Rami Hilles, an anti-Hamas Palestinian armed group operating with Israeli support, also increased. Between 30 June and 9 July, the group carried out three recorded incidents targeting IDP camps in Gaza city's At Tuffah and Shuja’iyya neighbourhoods, including reported abductions and raids, indicating increasingly complex security dynamics around the expanding Yellow Line.

The period preceding Israel's October 2026 elections has a high probability of reinforcing this trajectory rather than prompting a fundamental shift in military strategy. With far-right coalition partners Otzma Yehudit and Religious Zionism continuing to advocate expanding Israeli control over Gaza and negotiations on a durable ceasefire and post-conflict governance remaining stalled, the Likud-led caretaker government, in place since the Knesset dissolved on 17 July 2026, will very probably prioritise maintaining operational momentum in Gaza while avoiding the political and military risks associated with a large-scale offensive.

Territorial expansion is expected to continue through a combination of military and engineering measures that progressively transform temporary military positions into more permanent areas of control. Israeli forces are likely to continue advancing the Yellow Line through localised incursions supported by repeated evacuation orders, the demolition of buildings and agricultural land, and the construction of additional military infrastructure, including outposts, surveillance positions, access roads, trenches, and earthen barriers. Recent satellite imagery indicates that Israel has already constructed more than 23km of earth berms and trenches along parts of the Yellow Line, creating a fortified corridor that extends across central Gaza and, in some locations, beyond the original ceasefire demarcation. These measures are likely to be accompanied by the continued expansion of military exclusion zones and restrictions on civilian movement, allowing Israeli forces to consolidate control without undertaking a single large-scale offensive. ([BIPP 06/03/2026](https://www.bakerinstitute.org/research/israeli-elections-cast-doubt-gaza-peace-plan), [NPR 23/07/2026](https://www.npr.org/2026/07/23/nx-s1-5891506/israel-will-hold-elections-this-fall-gadi-eisenkott-could-be-the-next-prime-minister), [Chatham House 22/07/2026](https://www.chathamhouse.org/2026/07/israels-general-election-will-be-no-other), [CNN 20/07/2026](https://edition.cnn.com/2026/07/20/middleeast/israel-far-right-settlements-gaza-intl), [The Conversation 24/07/2026](https://theconversation.com/as-israel-prepares-for-october-election-the-government-is-accelerating-its-land-grab-in-the-west-bank-and-gaza-288286), [DAWN 21/07/2026](https://dawnmena.org/israels-elections-will-not-end-its-genocidal-and-expansionist-policies/), [ACLED accessed 25/07/2026](https://acleddata.com/conflict-data/data-export-tool), [Haaretz 07/07/2026](https://www.haaretz.com/israel-news/israel-security/2026-07-07/ty-article/.premium/as-netanyahu-battles-for-votes-he-could-reignite-gaza-fighting/0000019f-390c-d62f-a39f-7d2c08a00000), [LWJ 19/10/2025](https://www.longwarjournal.org/archives/2025/10/profiles-of-anti-hamas-militias-in-the-gaza-strip.php), [AP accessed 01/08/2026](https://apnews.com/article/israel-gaza-yellow-line-barrier-ceasefire-941ed80f6d4398ce88916f6b08753dd8), [TOI 17/07/2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/knesset-votes-on-official-dispersal-of-parliament-wrapping-up-final-legislative-blitz/), [AJ 22/07/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/7/22/creeping-death-israel-weaponises-yellow-line-to-annex-gaza))

title: Renewed cross-border strikes collapse the 2022 Houthi–Saudi truce, driving new displacement, disrupting imports, and reducing humanitarian access across Yemen
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale:
On 13 July 2026, the Iran-backed de-facto authority (DFA) in the north of Yemen (also known as the Houthis) announced the end of a de facto period of de-escalation with Saudi Arabia and the Saudi-backed Internationally Recognized Government (IRG) of Yemen, increasing the risk of renewed cross-border and intra-Yemeni hostilities following a series of retaliatory actions. On the same day, the IRG said it had struck Sana'a International Airport to prevent an Iranian aircraft from landing, while the DFA accused Saudi Arabia of carrying out the attack. The DFA subsequently retaliated by launching missile and drone attacks against Abha International Airport, marking the first attack on Saudi territory since the 2022 truce. On 20 July, the DFA announced a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia, describing it as a response to Saudi restrictions on DFA-controlled airports and seaports. The DFA has already targeted several vessels, including two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea, in an attempt to enforce the blockade.
Fighting has also intensified between the DFA and the IRG along front lines in Al Hodeidah, Al Jawf, Ma’rib, and Ta’iz, predating but compounded by the deterioration in Saudi–Houthi relations. Saudi Arabia is the main IRG backer, and the deterioration in Saudi–Houthi relations has already prompted expanded military involvement. From 24–25 July, the Saudi-led coalition conducted strikes in Al Hodeidah, while the IRG air force struck DFA missile and drone launch sites and weapons facilities in Ma'rib and Al Jawf. These developments indicate that the escalation has expanded beyond isolated cross-border retaliation, increasing the risk of sustained intra-Yemeni conflict.
The first cross-border attack on Saudi Arabia since the truce is significant because it signals that both parties are becoming increasingly willing to use direct military force to pursue their objectives, weakening one of the key restraints that has sustained the de facto ceasefire. Both Saudi Arabia and the DFA have incentives to avoid a renewed large-scale conflict. Saudi Arabia seeks to protect its economic interests and avoid another costly war, while the DFA is unlikely to escalate unless it perceives increased Saudi military involvement or an opportunity to improve its strategic position. A miscalculation could trigger the renewal of conflict. Further attacks on Saudi territory or attempts to enforce a blockade of the Bab Al Mandab Strait would increase the likelihood of expanded or sustained Saudi and international military involvement in the Red Sea and Yemen. Saudi Arabia has already announced plans for a multinational maritime defence coalition on 30 July 2026.
Escalations between the DFA and Saudi Arabia would likely intensify fighting between the DFA and the Saudi-backed IRG, further restricting humanitarian access. Saudi air strikes on seaports and airports would disrupt commercial and humanitarian imports, triggering new displacement. Supply chain disruptions would increase commodity prices and erode purchasing power. Any disruption to shipping through the Bab Al Mandab Strait would also have cascading impacts on regional and global supply chains while aggravating needs in a country where over 22 million people require humanitarian assistance and 18.3 million are acutely food-insecure. ([OCHA 29/03/2026](https://yemen.un.org/en/312711-ocha-yemen-yemen-humanitarian-needs-and-response-plan-2026-march-2026), [JP 25/07/2026](https://www.jpost.com/middle-east/article-903606), [Reuters 24/07/2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/yemen-teeters-towards-renewed-war-shadow-iran-conflict-2026-07-24/), [ICG 17/07/2026](https://www.crisisgroup.org/qna/middle-east-north-africa/yemen-iran-saudi-arabia/yemens-de-facto-truce-risk-how-prevent-return-war), [AJ 05/07/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/7/5/at-least-15-yemeni-government-troops-killed-in-hodeidah-fighting), [The Guardian 23/07/2026](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/jul/23/houthis-claim-attack-ship-tanker-saudi-arabia-red-sea), [Reuters 23/07/2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/houthis-say-they-attacked-saudi-tankers-red-sea-threatening-new-chokepoint-iran-2026-07-23/), [Arab News 25/07/2026](https://www.arabnews.com/node/2652234/middle-east), [SPA 25/07/2026](https://www.spa.gov.sa/en/N2640956))
hazard_materialisation:
Intense clashes between DFA and IRG forces spread across several Yemeni front lines, including Al Hodeidah, Ta’iz, Ma’rib, Al Jawf, Al Bayda, Al Dali’ and Lahj, with the heaviest fighting concentrated along the Red Sea coast and in Ta’iz. September was Yemen’s deadliest month since 2015, with over 4,000 reported fatalities. DFA territorial advances included capturing Al Mokha and positions near Bab Al Mandab, while subsequent IRG counteroffensives retook territory around Dhubab. The DFA also intensified cross-border missile and drone attacks against Saudi Arabia, targeting airports, oil facilities and energy infrastructure, including the East–West oil pipeline, while attempting to prevent Saudi oil shipments from transiting Bab Al Mandab. Saudi Arabia responded with airstrikes against DFA positions in Yemen. By October, DFA advances towards Ta’iz city, including the capture of Al Turba, had effectively placed the city under siege.

impact_materialisation_description:
The escalation has caused widespread displacement, disrupted essential services and aggravated food insecurity. By 31 October 2026, approximately 300,391 people had been displaced since June, mainly to Ta’iz, Lahj and Aden. The siege of Ta’iz has severely restricted civilian movement and humanitarian access, leaving over 600,000 people dependent on assistance beyond reach. Health services have deteriorated, with 42 facilities in Ta’iz city reporting critical shortages of fuel, oxygen and medicines. Insecurity and displacement have disrupted access to healthcare and education, while overcrowded displacement sites face heightened disease risks. Across Yemen, rising fuel and freight costs, maritime insecurity and disrupted supply routes have increased pressure on food prices and household purchasing power. Conflict-related livelihood losses and restrictions on market access have further reduced households' capacity to meet essential needs, particularly in frontline areas already experiencing severe food insecurity.

title: Renewed violence in As Sweida or settler outpost establishment drives Israeli expansion in southern Syria, displacing civilians and restricting access
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale:
Since the fall of Bashar Al Assad in December 2024, Israel’s military presence in southern Syria has evolved from incursions into sustained territorial control. By early 2026, Israeli forces have expanded beyond the UN-monitored 1974 separation line into parts of Quneitra and western Dar’a, establishing military posts, outposts, and checkpoints. By mid-2026, the presence had become increasingly entrenched, with regular patrols and ground activity beyond the former separation area. Further expansion of positions, checkpoints, or closed military zones would indicate movement towards a more permanent security zone. Sustained territorial control or restrictions on civilian access could increase local resistance and create conditions for further expansion towards areas linked to As Sweida.
Two pathways could accelerate or formalise this existing trajectory in the next three to six months. One is the revival of a proposal for a humanitarian corridor, first suggested in 2025 by Israeli officials to provide aid for Druze in As Sweida, particularly if renewed violence in As Sweida gives Israel a justification to intervene on behalf of the Druze and expand in southern Syria. The proposed corridor would connect the governorate with the Golan area, including Hader near Mount Hermon and Druze villages along the Syrian Golan. Although the proposal was previously rejected by the Syrian transitional Government, renewed violence or deterioration in As Sweida could bring it back into discussions and provide a pretext for expanding Israeli control or establishing protected access through southern Syria. While Israel framed its military intervention during the July 2025 violence as protecting the Druze, Druze opinion remains divided. One senior spiritual leader, Sheikh Hikmat Al Hijri, has welcomed Israeli involvement, while the other two have consistently rejected foreign interference, and As Sweida's Druze security chief warned it had complicated reconciliation.
A second pathway is the activity of Israeli settlers seeking to establish a permanent presence. The Pioneers of Bashan,  an Israeli settler movement, have repeatedly attempted to cross into southern Syria and establish outposts, including around Hader and Mount Hermon, with their stated ambitions extending across As Sweida, Dar'a, and Quneitra governorates. More than 40 settlers entered the outskirts of Hader in April, while approximately 70–100 attempted to cross through Mount Hermon in July, followed by further attempts in August. Armed Conflict Location & Event Data indicates an upward trend in incursion attempts since April 2026, peaking sharply in July with six recorded events. Although the Israel Defense Forces have so far prevented permanent settlement, repeated attempts could increase pressure on Israeli authorities to eventually formalise such activity.
If either pathway materialises, further Israeli control and presence in southern Syria are likely to restrict civilian movement and access to agricultural land through additional checkpoints, patrols, and military restrictions. An expanded Israeli presence could also prompt resistance from Syrian government forces, as well as communities or armed groups in Quneitra and western Dar'a, increasing the probability of clashes around Israeli positions. ([Ynet 20/08/2025](https://www.ynet.co.il/news/article/bktp9qfyxx), [Ynet 16/09/2025](https://www.ynet.co.il/news/article/hyhslcujxx), [Jewish Policy Center 01/10/2025](https://www.jewishpolicycenter.org/2025/10/01/focus-on-the-druze/), [AA 31/07/2025](https://www.aa.com.tr/en/middle-east/israeli-finance-minister-calls-for-humanitarian-corridor-to-syria-s-suwayda-for-druze-community/3646880), [Reuters 26/09/2025](https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/israel-syria-talks-hit-snag-over-humanitarian-corridor-sources-say-2025-09-26/), [AP 29/07/2026](https://apnews.com/article/israel-syria-netanyahu-jewish-settlers-bashan-461c4c4f686d5cf74f0617a7e70ffa29), [TOI 29/07/2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/fringe-settler-group-sneaking-into-syria-in-bid-to-claim-land-for-jewish-outpost/), [TOI 11/08/2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/three-settlement-activists-illegally-enter-syria-overnight-are-detained-by-idf/), [L'Orient Today 14/07/2026](https://today.lorientlejour.com/article/1541299/who-are-the-bashan-pioneers-the-israeli-settlers-eyeing-southern-syria.html), [Arab News 06/07/2026](https://www.arabnews.com/node/2649854/amp), [SOHR 27/06/2026](https://www.syriahr.com/en/383771/), [Enab Baladi 25/08/2026](https://english.enabbaladi.net/archives/2026/08/jordan-talks-fail-to-halt-israeli-incursions-in-southern-syria/), [EUAA accessed 28/07/2026](https://dip-aws.euaa.europa.eu/syria-security-situation/2142-territorial-control-and-main-armed-actors), [ACLED accessed 30/08/2026](https://acleddata.com/conflict-data/data-export-tool), [FP 24/07/2025](https://foreignpolicy.com/2025/07/24/risks-israel-druze-policy-syria/))

title: Military operations to secure the Dawei Special Economic Zone cause further forced displacement and severe protection risks in Dawei district, Tanintharyi region
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale:
By 28 August 2026, an estimated 700–1,000 military personnel were conducting clearance operations around the long-stalled Dawei Special Economic Zone (SEZ) in Yebyu township after a late-June order to protect the strategic projects. Since 9 July, fighting, raids, arson, looting, arbitrary arrests, and killings have displaced more than 4,500 people from eight Nabule villages. Renewed fighting near the SEZ from 21–22 August caused further civilian displacement. More than 2,000 people were displaced from ten villages in Thayetchaung township in August.
The concentration of military deployments around the project area, following orders to protect strategic infrastructure and agreements to revive the project, indicates that the operation is intended to secure the SEZ. The SEZ is a long-stalled port and industrial zone planned to include a deep-sea port, coal-fired power plant, oil refinery, and liquefied natural gas facilities. The risk is more immediate because Myanmar and Russia revived the project in 2025, signed a June 2026 power plant agreement, and included the Dawei port, refinery, and power plant in their August Moscow agreements. The timing of these deals and the deployment, alongside clashes with the Karen National Liberation Army (KNLA) near Wet Chaung, makes control of the project area a current strategic objective rather than a remote development scenario.
Over the next six months, military efforts to secure the SEZ are likely to include attempts to control Highway 8, the main north–south route through Tanintharyi, and the Dawei–Htee Khee road, which connects the project area through Myitta to the Thailand border. These routes are important for moving troops and supplies and would support future port and SEZ operations. Continued resistance activities by the KNLA, National Unity Government-affiliated People’s Defence Forces, and other local resistance groups operating in and around the Dawei SEZ could trigger further military sweeps, preventing safe returns and causing new and repeated displacement. Prolonged separation from homes, farms, and plantations will reduce food production and household income, increasing dependence on markets and host communities and worsening food, shelter, and health needs.
